prompt: Explain material, immaterial and institutional infrastructure.
solution:
Jochimsen's classification, which the lecture follows, splits infrastructure into three types:

Material infrastructure — the totality of all facilities, equipment and resources of an economy that serve energy supply, transport and telecommunications, i.e. the physical capital stock. Pipelines, power lines, substations, storage caverns, roads, ports, LNG terminals.

Institutional infrastructure — the evolved and established norms, institutions and procedures within which economic activity takes place: the legal framework, property rights, the regulatory authorities, standards and the market rules. In our field: the Energiewirtschaftsgesetz, the EU directives, the Bundesnetzagentur, unbundling rules, DVGW standards, the entry-exit market model.

Immaterial infrastructure — the number and characteristics of the individuals in the division of labour, with regard to their ability to contribute to the level and degree of integration of economic activity. In plain terms: human capital — education, qualification, know-how, health, mobility and willingness to work.

The point of the classification is that infrastructure is not only steel in the ground. A pipeline without a legal access regime and without engineers who can operate it produces nothing.

prompt: Assign five examples to the three categories of infrastructure.
solution:
Material infrastructure: a natural gas transmission pipeline; a 380 kV overhead line; an underground gas storage cavern; an LNG import terminal; a compressor station.

Institutional infrastructure: the Energiewirtschaftsgesetz (EnWG); the Bundesnetzagentur as regulatory authority; the unbundling rules of the EU internal market directives; the entry-exit market model and its capacity booking platform (PRISMA); the DVGW gas quality standards.

Immaterial infrastructure: the qualification of engineers and dispatchers who run the grid; the training and education system that produces them; the know-how of the operators; the health and mobility of the workforce; the willingness to cooperate across companies.

The safe way to sort an example: if you can trip over it, it is material. If it is a rule, a law or a body, it is institutional. If it sits in people's heads, it is immaterial.

prompt: The lecture lists the economic characteristics of infrastructure. Pick two of them and explain them.
solution:
The slide lists five: large investment projects with high capital requirements, external effects, economies of scale, step costs, and a high proportion of fixed costs. Two worth explaining:

Economies of scale. The average cost per transported unit falls as output grows, because the huge fixed cost of the asset is spread over more units and because the physics helps: the capacity of a pipe grows faster than its surface, so a larger diameter carries disproportionately more gas for the same metre of steel. This is what makes the grid a natural monopoly — one large operator is cheaper than two small ones — and is therefore the economic root of regulation.

Step costs. Capacity cannot be added continuously. You can build a 30-inch or a 36-inch pipeline, not a 33.7-inch one; a compressor comes in discrete sizes. Investment therefore comes in lumps, capacity jumps ahead of demand, and the new asset is under-utilised for years until demand grows into it. That is why infrastructure planning always argues over long horizons and why utilisation figures matter so much.

The other three, briefly: high capital requirements make financing and long amortisation periods a defining feature; external effects mean benefits and costs fall on third parties, which markets do not price; the high fixed-cost share means marginal cost pricing does not cover total cost, so a capacity charge is needed.

prompt: Name the types of compatibility that network nodes must provide, and give one example of each.
solution:
A network only works if the nodes are compatible with each other; compatibility is the prerequisite of every network. The lecture distinguishes three types:

1. Physical compatibility — the interface is a physical part of the product. Example: the flange and pressure class where two gas pipelines are coupled, or a plug that fits the socket.
2. Communication compatibility — the nodes speak a common transmission protocol. Example: the SCADA telemetry between dispatching centres, or the standardised nomination messages exchanged between transmission system operators.
3. Compatibility by convention — the interface works because the parties agreed on it, not because of physics. Example: a common currency, a common time reference such as the definition of the gas day, or an agreed gas quality band (Wobbe index).

Without compatibility at the nodes the individual lines stay isolated and the network effect — the value that grows with the number of connected participants — never materialises.

prompt: Why should transmission system operators be regulated?
solution:
Because transmission is a natural monopoly and therefore a monopolistic bottleneck. The cost function of a grid is sub-additive: one operator can serve the whole demand more cheaply than two, because the investment is huge, largely fixed and sunk, and economies of scale run right up to market size. Building a second parallel grid would waste capital, so competition *in* the network is not achievable — unlike production, trading and retail, where competition works perfectly well.

Left alone, the monopolist would restrict quantity, set monopoly prices and collect monopoly rents, and — if it is vertically integrated — deny or price out third-party access in order to protect its own sales business. The competitive stages upstream and downstream would then never develop.

Regulation is the answer: the state creates "as-if competition" for the bottleneck by determining network access and prices or quantities, and it enforces unbundling so that the grid is separated from the competitive stages. The political objective is lower prices for end customers; the expected result is more suppliers of the commodity and genuine competition in its sale, together with non-discriminatory third-party access, security of supply and the investment that a purely profit-driven monopolist would not make.

prompt: What is incentive-based regulation, and what is price-cap regulation?
solution:
The lecture splits regulatory procedures into two families:

Cost-based regulation — rate-of-return and cost-plus. The allowed revenue is derived from the company's own costs, so the regulated firm is reimbursed for what it spends.

Incentive-based regulation — price cap, revenue cap and yardstick competition. The allowed price or revenue is set in advance and decoupled from actual costs, so every euro the company saves stays with it. That is the incentive: cost reduction becomes profitable instead of pointless.

Price-cap regulation sets a ceiling for the price of the regulated service over a regulatory period, usually with an RPI − X formula: the cap may rise with inflation but must fall by a productivity factor X each year. Advantages: strong incentive for efficiency, low information requirement for the regulator, no direct cost audit. Problems: the quality of service can be cut to save money, so quality regulation has to be added; the company may earn very high profits if X was set too low, which is politically hard to defend and may be answered with a profit-sharing factor — but that in turn reduces the incentive for cost reduction.

Revenue cap works the same way on total revenue instead of price, which removes the incentive to sell more volume. Yardstick competition benchmarks each company against the others and gives continuous incentives, but assumes timely implementation and invites coordination between the regulated firms.

prompt: What is the Averch-Johnson effect, and in which context does it belong?
solution:
Context: it is the classic weakness of rate-of-return regulation, i.e. of cost-based regulation — the opposite family to the incentive-based procedures.

Under rate-of-return regulation the company may earn a fixed permitted return on its invested capital. The company therefore maximises profit subject to an upper limit on the return on capital. Since profit is a percentage of the capital base, the way to earn more is to make the capital base larger: the firm over-invests, uses excessive capital and distorts the factor mix towards capital and away from labour and operating expenditure. That systematic gold-plating is the Averch-Johnson effect.

The lecture lists it together with the other issues of rate-of-return regulation: no incentive for a more efficient factor allocation or for reducing operating costs, and information and control problems in implementation — the regulator can hardly tell a necessary investment from an unnecessary one.

The answer to it is incentive-based regulation: decouple the allowed revenue from the company's own costs (price cap, revenue cap, yardstick competition), so that neither over-investment nor inflated operating costs pay off.

prompt: Quote Jochimsen's definition of infrastructure and explain what economic function it ascribes to infrastructure. Which three types does the lecture derive from it, and what terminological inconsistency should you notice on this slide?
solution:
Jochimsen (1966, Theorie der Infrastruktur, p. 145) defines infrastructure as the entirety of material, institutional and personnel facilities and conditions available to the division-of-labour economy. Its function: it contributes to ensuring that equal factor payments are made for equal factor services with a purposeful allocation of resources.

That function is the examinable part. Infrastructure is what makes an economy behave as one single market instead of many isolated ones. If transport, grids, legal rules and qualified people are available everywhere, the same unit of labour or capital earns the same return wherever it is employed, and resources flow to where they are most productive. Infrastructure is therefore justified by an allocation and equalisation argument, not by the profitability of the individual asset - which is exactly why so much of it is publicly provided, publicly financed or regulated.

The three types the lecture derives are material infrastructure, institutional infrastructure and immaterial infrastructure.

The inconsistency: the definition on this very slide speaks of material, institutional and *personnel* facilities, while the list of types underneath calls the third one *immaterial*. Jochimsen's original triad is materielle / institutionelle / personelle Infrastruktur. Both labels denote the same thing here - the people and their qualification, i.e. human capital - but if the exam asks for 'the three types of infrastructure', answer with the lecture's own list: material, institutional, immaterial.

prompt: A natural monopoly is a market situation in which a single supplier can serve the relevant market at lower costs than several suppliers; formally it is a property of the cost function, which is then called ___.
solution: Sub-additive. The lecture is explicit that the natural monopoly is a characteristic of the cost function, not of the firm or of its behaviour. It is often the result of high fixed costs together with low marginal costs and is often associated with economies of scale: total costs for providing the good are lower when only one company offers it.

prompt: Write down the formal condition for a sub-additive cost function and explain in words what it says.
solution:
Let C(x) be the cost function for producing output x. The cost function is sub-additive if, for any two outputs a and b:

C(a+b) ≤ C(a) + C(b)

In words: the total cost of producing the combined output of two or more processes is less than or equal to the sum of the costs of producing each output separately. Producing a and b together never costs more than producing them apart, and usually costs less.

Sub-additivity reflects economies of scale or synergies in production — shared fixed assets, shared overhead, better utilisation of an indivisible plant. It indicates efficiency gains when resources are used in combination, and that is exactly why splitting a grid between two operators would raise total cost rather than lower it.

Watch the direction of the argument in an exam: economies of scale are a sufficient but not a necessary condition for sub-additivity in the single-product case, and economies of scope alone are not sufficient. Sub-additivity is the definition; the others are causes that often produce it.

prompt: The slide shows a chain from cost structure to regulation. Reproduce that chain and explain each arrow.
solution:
The chain reads: sub-additive cost function → natural monopoly → risk of monopoly rents → unbundling of vertically integrated companies → sector-specific regulation.

First arrow: the cost function is sub-additive — driven by economies of scope, economies of scale and sunk costs — which by definition makes the activity a natural monopoly.

Second arrow: a monopolist without competitive pressure can raise price above cost. The result is the risk of monopoly rents and thus disadvantages for customers. Note that the slide phrases it as a risk, not a certainty: the monopoly itself is efficient, it is the pricing behaviour that is the problem.

Third arrow: if the monopolist is also active in the competitive stages, it can use control of the bottleneck to disadvantage rivals there. The answer is unbundling — separating the vertically integrated company so that the network is not run by a party with an interest in who uses it.

Fourth arrow: separation alone does not set the price of network access, so the remaining monopoly is regulated sector by sector.

The important nuance: the aim is never to break the natural monopoly, because that would raise costs. The aim is to stop it being exploited.

prompt: Sketch the trilemma of energy policy and mark the IDEAL case in it. Name the three axes, say where the ideal polygon lies on each of them, and explain why the three goals form a trilemma rather than a simple list of aims.
solution:
The figure is a triangle spanned by three goals, one per axis: security of supply, sustainability and price. Each axis runs from 'low' in the centre of the triangle to 'high' at the corner.

The IDEAL polygon reaches out to 'high' on the security-of-supply axis and to 'high' on the sustainability axis, but stays in the centre, at 'low', on the price axis. In words: supply is always available, the system is clean, and energy is cheap at the same time.

It is a trilemma because the three goals are in conflict pairwise, so improving one normally costs one of the others. More sustainability means building renewables, storage and grids, which raises the price; more security of supply means redundant capacity, reserves and diversified import routes, which again raises the price; pushing the price down means cheap fuel, thin reserve margins and no premium for low emissions, i.e. it eats into both other corners. Energy policy therefore never optimises one number, it chooses a point inside the triangle, and regulation is the instrument that fixes the weighting.

(Note: the slide's heading contains the typo 'Security of Suply'.)

prompt: Compare the '(currently) REAL' trilemma figure with the IDEAL one of the previous slide. Which corner has moved, in which direction, and what does that say about the current state of the European energy system?
solution:
In the IDEAL figure the polygon is stretched out to 'high' on the security-of-supply and sustainability axes but pulled back to the centre, i.e. to 'low', on the price axis.

In the REAL figure the polygon is pulled outwards along the price axis: the price is high, not low. At the same time the polygon no longer reaches the corners on the other two axes - security of supply sits at a medium level and sustainability only reaches roughly the middle of its axis. The area of the real polygon is visibly smaller and lopsided towards the expensive corner.

Reading: the system currently pays a high price and gets neither full security of supply nor full sustainability in return. The gap between the two figures is the political agenda - it is the reason for market design changes, for network regulation and for the subsidy and tendering instruments the Bundesnetzagentur administers. The picture also shows why the trilemma is drawn at all: every measure that pushes one corner outwards has to be paid for on another axis.

prompt: Name the four levels of energy the lecture distinguishes, in the right order, and explain what is lost between each of them. Illustrate the chain with one example running from lignite to light.
solution:
The order is: primary energy - secondary energy - end energy - usable energy.

Primary energy carriers occur naturally and have not been subjected to any conversion: coal, lignite, crude oil, natural gas, uranium and the renewable sources.

Secondary energy carriers are the result of a conversion process in power plants, refineries or coking plants and are obtained from primary energy with conversion losses: coke, briquettes, electricity, district heating, heating oil, gasoline.

End energy is the energy consumed by the user, i.e. secondary (or directly primary) energy reduced by conversion and distribution losses - the kWh on the electricity meter, the litre of heating oil in the tank.

Usable energy is what is available after the final conversion in the devices of the end consumer: light, mechanical work, heat at the required temperature.

Example: lignite in the open-cast mine (primary) becomes electricity in the power plant at roughly 40 % efficiency (secondary), arrives at the socket after grid losses (end energy) and leaves the lamp as light (usable energy). Every arrow costs efficiency, which is why usable energy is only a small fraction of the primary input - and why saving one unit of usable energy saves several units of primary energy. That leverage is the whole argument for efficiency measures at the consumer end.

prompt: Define economies of scale and distinguish internal from external economies of scale. Give one energy-infrastructure example of each.
solution:
Economies of scale are the cost advantages a business achieves as a result of an increase in its level of production or output: as more units are produced, the average cost of production per unit tends to decrease.

Internal economies of scale result from factors within the firm - increased specialization, improved technology, better utilization of resources and increased bargaining power with suppliers. Example: a transmission system operator running 35,000 km of line spreads its control centre, its dispatching staff and its maintenance fleet over far more kilometres than a small operator, and it orders transformers in quantities that earn a discount.

External economies of scale occur outside the firm and are usually industry-specific: a whole industry benefits from a skilled labour force or from improved infrastructure in a particular region. Example: the cluster of pipeline engineering, welding and inspection firms in the Ruhr area, or a port region where LNG know-how, dredged channels and berths already exist, so that every additional terminal built there is cheaper than a greenfield one.

The purpose of both is the same - increase profit and market share. In infrastructure, economies of scale running up to the size of the market are the economic root of the natural monopoly.

prompt: The slide puts two figures for the USA next to each other. Describe what each of them shows and explain the tension between them.
solution:
Left figure: infrastructure investment as a percentage of GDP in the USA, annually from 1957 to 2019 (BEA fixed asset accounts, Deloitte Insights). It starts around 3.0 % in the late 1950s and declines over decades in a saw-tooth pattern to roughly 2.0 %, with a trough below 1.8 % in the early 1990s and a local peak around 2009, the post-crisis stimulus. The message: the United States has been under-investing in its physical stock for two generations relative to the size of its economy.

Right figure: the Bipartisan Infrastructure Deal, signed into law by President Biden in November 2021, opens $550 billion for new federal investments in transportation, broadband and utilities. Of this, $112.5 billion goes to public transport, split into $66 billion to reform rail services, $39 billion to modernise public transit, $5 billion for zero- and low-emission buses and $2.5 billion to improve ferry services.

The tension: $550 billion sounds enormous, but measured against a GDP of roughly $23 trillion and spread over several years it amounts to well under one percentage point of GDP per year. It slows the decline in the left-hand curve; it does not reverse it. That is the transferable lesson - headline infrastructure packages must be normalised by GDP and by the number of years before they can be judged, exactly as the German grid investment figures have to be read against the size of the grid.

prompt: Give the general definition of a price and name the four dimensions along which a price has to be specified before it means anything.
solution:
Price = monetary compensation divided by scope of services. A number on its own is not a price; it is only a price once it is clear what is being bought for it.

The four dimensions:
1. Scope of service — what shall be priced? The components of the service have to be defined in detail.
2. Location — where does which price apply? Prices at different locations are determined separately.
3. Time — when does which price apply? Prices at different points in time are defined separately.
4. Other restrictions — any further conditions limiting the validity of the price.

This structure is what makes the later gas chapters computable. An entry-exit tariff specifies scope (booked capacity), location (a named entry or exit point), time (per year or per day) and restrictions (firm or interruptible). Miss any one of the four and the same figure can mean two different things — which is exactly the trap in the ambiguity-of-storage-prices example later on.

prompt: The slide sorts German energy law into blocks. Name the three sector-specific blocks, give two examples for each, and say where the EnWG and its ordinances belong.
solution:
The figure has three sector-specific columns plus a column of general rules:

1. Competition law (WettbR): the EC Treaty (EGV), the Act against Restraints of Competition (GWB), the vertical block exemption regulation (VertikalVO) and the VWG. This is the general antitrust layer that applies to energy companies like to anyone else.

2. Energy law in the narrow sense (EnergieR i. e. S.): the European electricity and gas directives (EltRL, GasRL), the acceleration directive (Beschleunigungsrichtlinie Elt/Gas) and the third package, and on the German side the Energiewirtschaftsgesetz (EnWG) with its ordinances - StromNZV and GasNZV (network access conditions), StromNEV and GasNEV (network tariffs), NAV/NDAV (connection), ARegV (incentive regulation ordinance), Strom/GasGVV (basic supply), AVBFernwaermeV, KAV and MessZV. Alongside stand EnSG, AtG, the Grid Code and the Distribution Code.

3. Energy environmental law (EnergieumweltR): StromStG and MinOeStG (electricity and mineral oil tax), KWKModG (cogeneration) and EEG/EEWaermeG (renewables).

The EnWG is the centre of the middle column: it is the framework act, and the detailed rules that a network operator actually works with - access conditions, tariff calculation, the incentive regulation formula - are in the ordinances hanging below it. The general column (BGB, PAngVO) applies on top of everything, since a gas contract is still a contract.

prompt: The table lists four different reference conditions for gas volumes. Name them with their temperatures and the countries that use them, and calculate by how much the same amount of gas differs in cubic metres between the German norm condition and the European standard condition.

Define the Wobbe index, give its formula and explain why it, rather than the calorific value, decides whether two gases can be exchanged. Use the table to reconstruct the gross calorific value of methane from its Wobbe index and its relative density.
solution:
The Wobbe index is the parameter for the exchangeability of gases. It is defined as

Ws,n = Hs,n / sqrt(d)

with Hs,n the specific gross calorific value (Brennwert) of the gas and d = rho_ngas / rho_nLuft its relative density, i.e. the density of the gas divided by the density of air at the same reference condition.

Why this combination and not the calorific value alone: a burner is a fixed nozzle at a fixed supply pressure. The volume flow through a nozzle scales with 1/sqrt(density), and the heat released is that volume flow times the calorific value - so the heat output is proportional to H/sqrt(d), which is exactly the Wobbe index. Two gases with the same Wobbe index release the same heat at the same burner and the same pressure, even if their compositions and their calorific values differ. That is why gas specifications are written as a Wobbe band, and why H-gas and L-gas, whose Wobbe indices do not overlap, need separate networks or appliance readjustment.

Calculation for methane. The table gives Ws,n = 53.47 MJ/Nm3 and a relative density of 0.555. Then
Hs,n = Ws,n * sqrt(d) = 53.47 * sqrt(0.555) = 53.47 * 0.745 = 39.8 MJ/Nm3,
which is the familiar gross calorific value of methane (about 11.1 kWh/Nm3). Checking the other rows: ethane 68.70, propane 81.13 and n-butane 92.66 MJ/Nm3 gross - the Wobbe index rises with the carbon number, which is why adding LPG to a lean gas is the standard way of raising the Wobbe index of a gas that is too poor.

(Careful with the table: the column headed rho_n contains the relative density d - the dimensionless ratio to air - not the absolute density, which for methane would be 0.717 kg/m3.)

prompt: Read the DVGW G 260/I table for the 2nd gas family: give the Wobbe index ranges and nominal values for group L and group H, the gross calorific value range, the relative density range and the connection pressure. What does the small 'Schwankungsbereich' row regulate?
solution:
DVGW G 260/I, 2nd gas family (natural gas), at pn = 1013.25 hPa and Tn = 273.15 K:

Wobbe index Ws,n, total range:
- group L: 10.5 to 13.0 kWh/m3, i.e. 37.8 to 46.8 MJ/m3;
- group H: 12.8 to 15.7 kWh/m3, i.e. 46.1 to 56.5 MJ/m3.
Nominal value: group L 12.4 kWh/m3 (44.6 MJ/m3), group H 15.0 kWh/m3 (54.0 MJ/m3).

Gross calorific value Hs,n, for both groups: 8.4 to 13.1 kWh/m3, i.e. 30.2 to 47.2 MJ/m3.
Relative density d: 0.55 to 0.75.
Connection pressure pan: total range 18 to 24 mbar, nominal value 20 mbar - the pressure at the appliance, which is what makes the Wobbe index the right yardstick in the first place.

The 'Schwankungsbereich im oertlichen Versorgungsgebiet' row is the tighter rule that actually binds the network operator: within one local supply area the Wobbe index may deviate from the value the appliances are set to by only +0.6 / -1.4 kWh/m3 (group L) and +0.7 / -1.4 kWh/m3 (group H). The wide total range describes which gases may exist somewhere in Germany; the narrow fluctuation band describes how much the gas in one town may move without anyone having to visit the burners. Note that the ranges of L and H overlap slightly (12.8 to 13.0 kWh/m3), but the nominal values, 12.4 against 15.0, are far apart - which is why an L-gas area cannot simply be fed with H-gas.

prompt: According to DVGW G 260/I the nominal Wobbe index of group H gas is 15.0 kWh/m3, while for group ___ gas it is only 12.4 kWh/m3.
solution: Group L (L-gas, low calorific value). The total ranges are 10.5 to 13.0 kWh/m3 for L and 12.8 to 15.7 kWh/m3 for H; the nominal values are 12.4 and 15.0 kWh/m3 respectively. Both groups share the same gross calorific value range of 8.4 to 13.1 kWh/m3 and the same relative density band of 0.55 to 0.75, and both are supplied at a nominal connection pressure of 20 mbar.

prompt: The lecture decomposes the 'product' natural gas into two parts. Name them, name the elements of flexibility, and explain why a customer buys the second part at all.
solution:
The product natural gas consists of a commodity part and a flexibility part, and on top of that supplementary products can be sold.

The commodity is the energy itself - so many kWh of gas, indifferent to when they are delivered.

The flexibility is the right to take those kWh when the customer actually needs them. Its elements are transportation, storage, production flexibility and interruptibility. Transportation moves the gas from where it is to where the customer is, storage moves it from summer to winter, production flexibility lets the field swing its output, and interruptibility is the mirror image - the customer accepts being cut off in exchange for a lower price, so the supplier gains flexibility from him.

The customer buys flexibility because his demand is not flat. Space heating follows the temperature, industrial processes follow the shift plan, and a power plant follows the merit order. A pure commodity contract with a flat delivery profile would force him to store or to waste. On the supply side, flexibility is what the seller can charge for beyond the raw energy - which is why the value chain contains storage and transport as separate businesses at all.

The slide also frames the competition: gas competes as a feedstock and as a fuel with crude oil or oil products, coal and other fuels, and its uses run from feedstock and heating through industrial processes and electricity production to transport.
section: Natural gas: value chain and properties

prompt: Sketch the temperature-correlated consumption profile and label it. Explain the difference between quantity, flow and capacity in the figure, and what ACQ, QCQ and MCQ stand for.
Using a sketch, explain what compressor stations are needed for.
solution:
Sketch: pressure on the vertical axis, distance along the pipeline on the horizontal axis. The pressure falls along the line because of friction — a sawtooth: it drops steadily, then jumps back up at each compressor station, drops again, and so on. Mark the minimum pressure the line must not fall below and the maximum design pressure.

What compressors do: they maintain the pressure. Gas flows only along a pressure gradient, and friction eats that gradient, so without re-compression the throughput would collapse after a few hundred kilometres. Lecture figures: pipelines up to 6,000 km long, diameter up to 1,400 mm, pressure up to 100 bar, compressor spacing 80 to 500 km, driven by natural gas or electricity, consuming up to about 0.5 % of the throughput per 100 km.

The economics: transport capacity can be bought either with more steel (a larger diameter) or with more compression (more stations). Both cost money, so the design is an economic compromise between the number of compressors and the pipeline diameter — the optimisation slide shows the same capacity realised as 44″ with few stations or 34″ with many. The cost of the energy for compression can dominate the trade-off. Compressors are also needed at storage facilities to inject gas against reservoir pressure.

prompt: Draw the LNG value chain and say which steps cause the highest costs.
solution:
The chain, left to right, five stages:

1. Exploration & production — find the field, produce and treat the gas.
2. Refrigeration & liquefaction — remove CO2, water, H2S and heavy hydrocarbons, then cool to about −162 °C. The volume shrinks by roughly a factor of 600. This is the liquefaction train, the capital-intensive heart of the chain.
3. Transportation — loading and shipping in LNG carriers (Moss spherical or membrane tanks), with boil-off gas used as fuel.
4. Storage & regasification — the import terminal: LNG tanks, vaporisers, feed-in into the receiving grid.
5. Customer.

Cost breakdown from the lecture's slide: exploration and production 11 %, refrigeration and liquefaction 42 %, transportation 20 %, storage and regasification 27 %.

So the answer to the second half: liquefaction is by far the most expensive step at 42 %, followed by storage and regasification at 27 %. The sea leg itself, at 20 %, is comparatively cheap — and that is exactly why LNG beats pipelines over long distances: the expensive parts sit at the two ends and do not grow with distance.
slide_title: Costs along the LNG Value Chain

prompt: Why can it be more advantageous to transport natural gas as LNG than through a pipeline?
solution:
The decisive argument is the cost structure over distance. Pipeline cost rises roughly linearly with distance: every additional kilometre needs more steel, more right of way and, every 80–500 km, another compressor station. The LNG chain instead carries very high fixed costs at the two ends — the liquefaction plant (42 % of the chain cost) and storage/regasification (27 %) — while the sea leg itself is comparatively cheap (20 %) and barely grows with distance. The two cost curves therefore cross: beyond a break-even distance LNG is cheaper. On the lecture's ENI chart LNG (roughly 2–2.5 US$/MMBtu, almost flat) undercuts an offshore pipeline from about 1,000 miles and a low-pressure onshore pipeline from roughly 3,000 miles; only a high-pressure onshore line stays competitive out to about 4,500 miles.

Beyond cost there are strategic advantages: LNG is not tied to a fixed route and is therefore flexible — it diversifies supply, opens markets no pipeline reaches, avoids transit countries and the political and geographic restrictions that come with them, and cargoes can be re-directed to whichever market pays most (arbitrage). Pipelines in turn win at short distance, high and steady volumes and where a stable long-term relationship between two countries already exists.
note: The memory protocol writes "LNG (gaseous)" — that is wrong. LNG is liquefied natural gas, cooled to about −162 °C, which shrinks its volume by a factor of roughly 600 and is exactly what makes sea transport possible.

prompt: Calculate the cost of reserving transport capacity for one year under an entry-exit pricing system.
solution:
In an entry-exit system the shipper books capacity at an entry point and, independently, at an exit point; there is no route and no distance in the tariff. Total cost = entry price · booked entry capacity + exit price · booked exit capacity, each converted to energy first.

κ_E = κ_V · GCV
C_TE = κ_E · p_Entry + κ_E · p_Exit · 365 (whenever the exit price is quoted per day)

Lecture example (slide 199): κ_V = 10,000 m³/h, GCV = 11 kWh/m³, p_Entry = 1.7 €/kWh/h/a, p_Exit = 0.00219178 €/kWh/h/d
κ_E = 10,000 · 11 = 110,000 kWh/h
C_TE = 110,000 · 1.7 + 110,000 · 365 · 0.00219178 = 187,000 + 88,000 = 275,000 €/a

The exam variant (slide 229) uses p_Entry = 2 €/kWh/h/a and p_Exit = 0.01 €/kWh/h/d:
Entry = 110,000 kW · 2 €/kW/a = 220,000 €/a
Exit = 110,000 kW · 0.01 €/kW/d · 365 d/a = 401,500 €/a
Total = 621,500 €/a

Two traps: convert m³/h into kWh/h before anything else, and check whether the price is per year or per day — the exit price usually is per day and has to be multiplied by 365. Contrast this with distance-related pricing (price · distance · capacity) and postage stamp pricing (price · capacity, one flat tariff for the whole network); entry-exit is the system that removes "pancaking" across several networks.

prompt: State the lecture's key figures for long-distance gas pipelines and their compressors. Then calculate how much of the transported gas a 4,000 km pipeline consumes for compression, and say what that means for the delivered quantity.
solution:
Key figures. Natural gas is transported by pipeline (gaseous), by ship (liquefied) and, less commonly, by vehicle (liquefied or gaseous). For pipelines: length up to 6,000 km, diameter up to 1,400 mm (occasionally more), pressure up to 100 bar. Compressors: their function is maintaining pressure; spacing 80 to 500 km; they are driven by natural gas or by electricity; consumption up to 0.5 % per 100 km of the transported natural gas, and highly variable.

Calculation for 4,000 km at the upper figure of 0.5 % per 100 km:
number of 100 km sections = 4,000 / 100 = 40
linear estimate: 40 * 0.5 % = 20 % of the transported gas is burned on the way.
Compounded, because each station takes its share of what is left: 0.995^40 = 0.818, i.e. 18.2 % consumed and 81.8 % delivered.

Meaning. Of 100 bcm injected, some 82 bcm arrive; the rest has been burned in the turbines. That is a fuel cost and a CO2 stream, and it is charged to the shipper as fuel gas. Three consequences follow:
- distance is expensive for gas in a way it is not for oil, which is why the transport-mode diagram hands long distances to LNG;
- electric drives instead of gas turbines move the emissions to the power sector and can be run on renewables;
- the compressor fuel is one half of the diameter-versus-compression trade-off: a larger diameter loses less pressure, so it needs fewer stations and burns less gas, at the price of more steel.
With an assumed 8 % compression loss the same arithmetic over 4,000 km would already justify a considerably larger pipe.

prompt: Compare the pipeline transport of a liquid with that of a gas using the pressure and velocity curves of the slide. Why do the two curves behave differently, and what does the energy content comparison add?
solution:
Left figure, liquid: along the distance the pressure p falls almost linearly and the velocity v stays constant. A liquid is practically incompressible, so its density does not change when the pressure drops; by continuity the same mass flow through the same cross-section must move at the same speed. Friction simply eats a constant amount of pressure per kilometre.

Right figure, gas: the pressure p falls slowly at first and then ever more steeply - the curve is concave and drops off at the end - while the velocity v rises, slowly at first and then sharply, crossing the pressure curve. A gas is compressible: as the pressure falls its density falls with it, so the same mass flow needs an ever larger volume flow, i.e. a higher velocity. The higher velocity in turn increases the friction losses, which accelerates the pressure drop further - a self-reinforcing effect. This is exactly why the pressure profile between two compressor stations is not a straight line, and why a line must not be run down to too low a pressure.

Energy content: 1 m3 of light fuel oil contains 9,900 kWh, 1 m3 of natural gas only 9.8 to 12.3 kWh. The ratio is 9,900 / 12.3 = 805 up to 9,900 / 9.8 = 1,010, i.e. a cubic metre of oil carries about 800 to 1,000 times the energy of a cubic metre of gas at atmospheric conditions.

Put together, the two halves explain gas transport economics. To move a comparable amount of energy you have to move about a thousand times the volume, and moving that volume costs velocity, friction and hence compression energy. Compression to 100 bar recovers most of the factor - it raises the density roughly a hundredfold - which is why gas lines run at high pressure, why liquefaction (a factor of about 600) is the answer for long distances, and why oil can be pumped over thousands of kilometres with far less energy per unit of energy delivered.

prompt: The chart plots transmission cost in EUR per cubic metre against hours per year for three pipeline diameters, 34, 38 and 44 inches. Explain the shape of the curves, say which diameter is cheapest in which region, and why the curves for the smaller diameters turn upward.
solution:
The x-axis is the number of hours per year during which gas actually flows; the caption states that the flow rate remains constant at 1.4 mln m3/h while the duration of flow increases, so moving to the right means more volume through the same pipe, i.e. a higher load factor. The y-axis is the cost per transported cubic metre, between about 0.01 and above 0.02 EUR/cbm.

Shape. On the left every curve is high because the pipeline's capital cost - steel, welding, right of way - is a fixed cost that has to be recovered from very few cubic metres. As the utilisation grows, the same fixed cost is spread over more volume, so all curves fall. That is the classic degression of a capital-intensive infrastructure.

Why the small diameters turn upward again: a 34-inch line can only push 1.4 mln m3/h through by running at a high gas velocity, and the friction loss grows with the square of the velocity. Beyond a certain throughput the additional compression energy - fuel gas or electricity, which is a variable cost - grows faster than the fixed cost per unit falls, so the curve has a minimum and then rises steeply. The 34-inch curve turns up earliest and most sharply, the 38-inch curve later and more gently, and the 44-inch curve is still falling at 8,000 h/a because it never has to be driven that hard.

Which diameter wins where: at low utilisation, roughly below 2,500-3,000 h/a, the 34-inch line is cheapest because its fixed cost is smallest; in the middle region the 38-inch line has the lowest cost; from about 4,000 h/a onwards the 44-inch line is cheapest and stays cheapest. The arrow labelled 'downstream' points from the large to the small diameters: the further downstream in the system you go, the smaller the pipe and the lower the load factor, which is exactly consistent with the curves.

Rule for the exam: high, steady throughput justifies a large diameter; low or seasonal throughput does not.
slide_title: Influence of Pipeline Diameter and Compression on Transmission Cost

prompt: The optimisation figure shows the same transport task over 200 km realised with three different diameters. How many compressor stations does each case need?
options: 44 inches needs four stations, 38 inches two, 34 inches one.
34 inches needs two stations, 38 inches four, 44 inches eight.
44 inches needs one station, 38 inches two, 34 inches four.
All three cases need two stations; only the pressure level differs.
solution:
Case 1, 44 inches: a single compressor station at kilometre 0, and the pressure sags only gently over the whole 200 km. Case 2, 38 inches: two stations, one at 0 and one at about 100 km. Case 3, 34 inches: four stations, i.e. roughly one every 50 km, each followed by a steep pressure decay.

The figure is the graphic form of Q ~ sqrt(p1^2 - p2^2 / L) * D^2.5: the narrower the pipe, the higher the velocity for the same throughput, the faster the pressure falls, and the sooner it has to be restored. The economic reading is that transport capacity can be bought either as steel or as compression - a large diameter with few stations, or a small diameter with many. Steel is capital expenditure paid once; compression is capital plus fuel gas or electricity paid every year, which is why the optimum shifts towards a larger diameter when energy is expensive or the load factor is high, and towards more compression when the line is used only intermittently.

prompt: The slide asks: "Transport or separate product?". Walk through the elements of the figure and then answer the question - is LNG just another way of transporting natural gas, or a product in its own right? Argue both readings.
solution:
The figure, left to right: gas fields feed gas processing facilities; a pipeline takes the treated gas to the liquefaction plant; it is stored in LNG tanks and loaded at the LNG loading terminal; an LNG carrier crosses the ocean; at the LNG terminal a carrier discharges into the receiving terminal's LNG tanks; regasification turns the liquid back into gas; a pipeline delivers it to gas utilities and to a power station.

Read as transport: gas goes in at one end and gas comes out at the other. Liquefaction is only a physical trick - cooling to about -162 °C shrinks the volume by a factor of roughly 600 - and it exists solely to make sea transport possible. Nothing is added to the commodity, and the chain competes with a pipeline for exactly the same job, which is why the lecture judges it on delivered cost over distance.

Read as a separate product: LNG is bought, sold, priced and shipped as a liquid in its own right. It has its own quality specification, its own price benchmarks, its own contract forms (FOB, DES, charterparties, heel, demurrage) and uses that pipeline gas cannot serve - ship bunkering, truck delivery to off-grid customers, small-scale LNG, power ships. Slide 161 makes this visible: the same molecule ends up at 7.8, 10.0 or 12.8 USD/MMBtu depending on which LNG product it becomes.

The lecture's answer is both: in the large-scale import business LNG is a transport option competing with pipelines; in the small- and medium-scale business it has become a product of its own.

prompt: This figure adds the modern, non-classical parts of the LNG chain. Name the four floating or small-scale concepts it shows and explain, for FLNG and FSRU, what problem each of them solves.
solution:
Besides the classical route (offshore gas platform or gas field, onshore LNG plant, ocean-going carrier, onshore receiving terminal, city), the figure shows four newer concepts: near-shore FLNG, open-sea FLNG, FSRU, and small-scale LNG including a power ship supplying a city directly.

FLNG (floating liquefied natural gas) is a liquefaction plant on a hull moored over or near the field. It solves the stranded-gas problem: a field that is too small, too remote or too deep to justify an offshore pipeline to shore plus an onshore plant plus a jetty. FLNG removes the pipeline to shore, the land acquisition and much of the permitting, and it can be moved to the next field when this one is depleted - so it converts an immovable, site-specific investment into a re-deployable asset.

FSRU (floating storage and regasification unit) is the mirror image on the import side: a ship with LNG storage and vaporisers that discharges gas straight into the grid at a jetty. It solves the time and commitment problem: an onshore regasification terminal takes years to build and is sunk once built, whereas an FSRU can be chartered and be on stream within months and released again afterwards. That is exactly why Germany used FSRUs in 2022/23 - and why the load factors of slide 170 matter, since a chartered FSRU costs its hire whether it regasifies or not.

Small-scale LNG and power ships extend the chain past the grid: LNG is delivered by small vessel, truck or ISO container to customers with no pipeline connection, at the higher costs shown on slide 161.

prompt: A ship that stores LNG and vaporises it directly into the receiving grid, so that no onshore regasification terminal has to be built, is called an ___.
solution: FSRU - floating storage and regasification unit. Its advantage over an onshore terminal is speed and reversibility: it can be chartered and commissioned within months and returned afterwards, instead of a multi-year, sunk investment. Its counterpart on the export side is the FLNG, a floating liquefaction plant. All six German import points listed on slide 164 were FSRUs ("schwimmend") before stationary terminals were planned for 2026/27.

prompt: The slide contrasts a pipeline route from Iran to Western Europe with the LNG route, under the heading "Political and geographic restrictions". Which statement describes the contrast correctly?
options: The pipeline route crosses six countries, each of which is a political risk and a possible transit fee; the LNG route avoids land borders but depends on a maritime chokepoint, the Suez Canal.
The pipeline route crosses no borders because it runs offshore, while the LNG route has to cross six national jurisdictions.
The LNG route is free of any geographic restriction, which is why LNG cost is independent of the origin of the cargo.
Both routes are politically identical; the only difference is that the LNG route is shorter.
solution: The slide's own title states it: pipeline Iran to Western Europe means six countries, LNG means the Suez Canal. Each transit country is a party that can interrupt the flow, levy a transit fee, or renegotiate the terms, and each one must agree before the line can even be built - which is why such projects usually fail politically rather than technically. LNG replaces that chain of countries with the open sea, but it does not remove geography: cargoes from the Gulf to Europe pass Hormuz and Suez, and a closure forces the long way round the Cape, which adds thousands of kilometres and days of charter hire. The second option inverts the two routes. The third ignores exactly the point of the slide. The fourth is wrong because LNG cost does depend on distance - only much more weakly than pipeline cost, as slide 160 shows.
slide_title: Pipeline: Iran – Western Europe: 6 countries LNG: Suez Canal

prompt: The ENI chart plots four pipeline cost lines and one LNG line against distance. Explain why there are four different pipeline lines and what determines their different slopes. Then explain the significance of the caption "for 10 x 10^9 m3/year capacity".
solution:
The four pipeline lines are two pairs. The first distinction is offshore versus onshore: the offshore line is by far the steepest, rising from under 1 USD per million Btu at 500 miles to about 4.4 at 2,600 miles, because laying pipe on the seabed needs specialised vessels, thicker walled and coated pipe, and gives no chance of intermediate compressor stations except on platforms. The second distinction, within the onshore family, is low pressure versus high pressure. A higher operating pressure carries more gas through the same diameter and stretches the distance between compressor stations, so the high-pressure line is the flattest of the four - it stays below the LNG line right out to 4,500 miles - while the low-pressure line reaches about 3.3 USD per million Btu at 4,500 miles and is overtaken by LNG at roughly 3,000 miles.

The slopes are therefore set by the cost of adding one more kilometre of transport capacity: steel and laying cost per kilometre plus the compression needed to overcome friction. The LNG line by contrast starts high, at about 1.8 to 2 USD per million Btu even at short distance, because liquefaction and regasification have to be paid regardless, and then rises only gently - the sea leg is cheap per kilometre.

The caption matters because the whole comparison is conditional on one capacity, 10 x 10^9 m3 per year. Both technologies have strong economies of scale, but not the same ones: pipeline specific cost falls with diameter roughly as capacity^(1/2.58 - 1), while the LNG chain scales with train and vessel size. Change the volume and all five lines move, and the break-even distances move with them. A cost comparison of transport options is therefore never a single number: it is always "at this capacity, over this distance, with this pressure and this route".

prompt: Using the numbers in this figure - feedgas 1 USD/MMBtu, liquefaction and regasification 2.8 USD/MMBtu, LNG shipping about 0.1 USD/MMBtu per 1,000 km - calculate the break-even distance against a pipeline tariff of 1.0 USD/MMBtu per 1,000 km and against one of 0.5 USD/MMBtu per 1,000 km. Compare your results with the two circles marked on the chart.
solution:
Set up both cost functions as a function of distance d, measured in thousands of km.

LNG: c_LNG(d) = feedgas + liquefaction and regasification + shipping = 1.0 + 2.8 + 0.1 d = 3.8 + 0.1 d [USD/MMBtu]. The intercept 3.8 is the green diamond on the chart at d = 0.
Pipeline: c_pipe(d) = feedgas + tariff x distance = 1.0 + t d, starting from the red diamond at 1.0.

Break-even: 3.8 + 0.1 d = 1.0 + t d, hence d = 2.8 / (t - 0.1).

Case 1, t = 1.0 USD/MMBtu per 1,000 km: d = 2.8 / 0.9 = 3.11, i.e. about 3,100 km. Check: pipeline 1.0 + 3.11 = 4.11, LNG 3.8 + 0.31 = 4.11 USD/MMBtu. That is the left-hand circle on the chart, at roughly 3,000 km and just above 4 USD/MMBtu.

Case 2, t = 0.5 USD/MMBtu per 1,000 km: d = 2.8 / 0.4 = 7.0, i.e. 7,000 km. Check: pipeline 1.0 + 3.5 = 4.5, LNG 3.8 + 0.7 = 4.5 USD/MMBtu. That is the right-hand circle, at about 7,000 km and 4.5 USD/MMBtu.

Interpretation: below the break-even distance the pipeline is cheaper, above it LNG is. The break-even is extremely sensitive to the pipeline tariff - halving the tariff from 1.0 to 0.5 more than doubles the break-even distance, from about 3,100 to 7,000 km. It is equally sensitive to the LNG end costs: if liquefaction and regasification could be built for 2.0 instead of 2.8 USD/MMBtu, the break-even against t = 1.0 would fall to 2.0/0.9 = 2,200 km. The chart's LNG shipping slope is itself an assumption - it corresponds to a long-term charter at 80,000 USD per day.

prompt: What exactly does a shipper buy when he pays a transport price, and what do the units €/(m³/h)/[km]/a and €/(kWh/h)/[km]/a tell you about the product? Explain the three remarks the slide adds: 'available: volume not energy', 'capacity ≠ utilization' and 'price ≠ cost'.
solution:
The scope of service is capacity, not gas. The shipper books a maximum flow that the transporter/carrier has to keep available for him: a volume (or energy) per time unit, at a defined point, for a defined period and — if the tariff is distance-related — over a defined length. That is why the unit has three parts: a flow (m³/h or kWh/h), possibly a length (km), and always a period (a). The two unit variants describe the same product; they are linked by the gross calorific value, κ_E = κ_V · GCV, and €/(kWh/h)/a is identical to €/kW/a, i.e. a capacity price.

Available: volume not energy — the pipeline physically moves cubic metres; how many kWh those carry depends on the gas quality, so the same m³/h booking delivers a different amount of energy for L-gas than for H-gas.

Capacity ≠ utilization — the shipper pays for the booked capacity whether or not gas flows. A booking used at 50 % costs exactly as much as one used at 100 %, so the specific transport cost in €/MWh doubles when utilisation halves. This is the fixed-cost logic of every network industry.

Price ≠ cost — what the shipper pays is a regulated or negotiated tariff, not the transporter's cost of producing the service; the two only coincide under strictly cost-based regulation, and incentive regulation deliberately drives a wedge between them.

The fourth remark, 'time-unit?', is the exam trap: a price may be quoted per year or per day. A price per day has to be multiplied by 365 before it can be added to an annual charge.

prompt: Transport capacity is physically available as a volume flow (m³/h), but tariffs are usually quoted per energy flow (kWh/h). The factor that converts the one into the other is the ___.
solution: The gross calorific value (GCV, Brennwert), quoted in kWh/m³. κ_E = κ_V · GCV, e.g. 10,000 m³/h · 11 kWh/m³ = 110,000 kWh/h = 110,000 kW = 110 MW. Every capacity calculation in this lecture starts with this conversion, because the booking is stated in m³/h while the price is quoted per kWh/h.

prompt: Name the three transportation pricing systems shown on the slide, give the calculation formula of each, and state for each system what the shipper's bill actually depends on.
solution:
1. Distance-related pricing: C = Price * Distance * Capacity. The shipper contracts a route through the network and pays for its length; the bill grows linearly with the distance (in the lecture example l1 + l2 + l3) and with the booked capacity.

2. Entry-exit pricing: C = (Entry-Price * Entry-Capacity) + (Exit-Price * Exit-Capacity). Entry and exit are booked and paid separately and independently. No route is contracted, so the bill does not depend on where the gas physically flows or how far it travels — only on which points are used and how much capacity is booked at each of them. This is the system used in the EU today; it is what makes a virtual trading point and free re-routing possible.

3. Postage stamp pricing: C = Price * Capacity. One uniform tariff for the whole network, exactly like a stamp on a letter: the same price whether the letter travels 10 km or 500 km. The bill depends only on the booked capacity.

All three are pricing systems, i.e. they say how the money is calculated, not which physical path the gas takes. In the lecture's three worked examples the same shipper (10,000 m³/h, GCV 11 kWh/m³) pays 275,000 €/a under every one of them — the systems are calibrated to the same revenue, and they differ in how that revenue is spread over shippers with different distances.

prompt: The lecture defines transportation as the "provision of capacity and related services at or between A and B during a defined term". Break this definition into its three components, name the two parties, and say what each of them actually contracts for.
solution:
Transportation is not the sale of gas, it is the sale of a service, and the definition has three components.

(1) Capacity and related services: what is sold is the right to a maximum flow (m3/h or kWh/h) that the transporter must keep available, plus the services that go with it - metering, receipt and confirmation of nominations, allocation, data management, billing.
(2) At or between A and B: the service is tied to points. A is the delivery point (also receipt point, point of acceptance, inlet point) where the shipper hands the gas over; B is the redelivery point (also point of delivery, outlet point) where he takes it back.
(3) During a defined term: every booking has a start and an end. Term is one of the four main contract clauses, together with capacity, price and location.

The two parties are the shipper, who reserves the transportation capacity and stays the owner of the gas from A to B, and the carrier or transporter, who owns and operates the pipeline and only moves the shipper's molecules. Because the shipper pays for the reserved capacity whether or not gas flows, capacity and utilisation must never be confused: a booking used at half load costs exactly as much as one used at full load, and the specific cost per MWh doubles.

prompt: The chart shows nominal liquefaction capacity by country for 2016 and 2022 plus the 2016 utilisation on the right-hand axis. Describe the three things it tells you, and explain what a utilisation figure near 100 % versus one near 0 % means for a liquefaction plant.
solution:
Three messages.

1. Concentration and its shift. In 2016 Qatar is by far the largest single exporter with roughly 77 MTPA, ahead of Australia at about 57 MTPA. In the 2022 projection Australia rises to about 88 MTPA and overtakes Qatar, which stays flat. The other established exporters - Algeria, Nigeria, Malaysia, Indonesia - barely move.

2. The new entrant. The United States goes from about 11 MTPA in 2016 to about 67 MTPA in 2022, the largest absolute increase of any country. Russia roughly triples from about 11 to about 28 MTPA. Growth is therefore concentrated in two countries, not spread across the world.

3. Utilisation varies enormously. The blue dots for 2016 run from essentially 0 % to over 100 %. The good performers - Qatar, Australia, Norway, Russia, Papua New Guinea, Malaysia - sit at or slightly above 100 %; the weak ones include several African plants (Angola at around 15 %, Cameroon effectively nothing) and the United States at roughly 48 %, since its first trains had only just started.

What that means: liquefaction is the capital-intensive heart of the chain, 42 % of the chain cost on slide 145, and it is almost entirely fixed cost. Specific cost is therefore inversely proportional to utilisation - a plant at 50 % load has roughly twice the specific liquefaction cost of the same plant at full load, which is what pushes a project up the global cost curve of slide 147. A figure near 100 % means the plant is earning its capital back as planned; a figure near 0 % means the capital is still being serviced while nothing is being produced, and the cause is normally not the plant itself but upstream feedgas shortage, civil unrest, or commissioning delay. Figures slightly above 100 % are normal and not an error: nameplate capacity is a design value and a well-run train can be over-fired, especially in cold ambient conditions.

prompt: The slide draws three consequences from the cost structure of pipelines. State them, explain the chain of reasoning that leads to "costs per unit of capacity decrease with increasing diameter", and point out where the slide's own wording is imprecise.
solution:
The statements on the slide: about 95 % of the costs are fixed; costs per length are proportional to diameter and capacity; capacity increases over-proportionally with diameter; therefore costs per unit of capacity decrease with increasing diameter. The 3D surface behind them shows total cost rising with both capacity and length.

The chain of reasoning. The cost of one kilometre of pipeline is essentially the cost of the steel and of laying it, and that grows roughly in proportion to the diameter D - a wall of given thickness wrapped around a larger circle. The throughput, however, does not grow with D: friction in a pipe falls as the pipe gets wider, so the flow that can be pushed through at a given pressure drop grows roughly with D^2.58 (that is the pipeline coefficient gamma = 2.58 of slide 177). Divide the one by the other: cost per unit of capacity behaves like D / D^2.58 = D^-1.58, i.e. it falls sharply as the pipe gets bigger. That is a pure economy of scale, and it is the technical origin of the natural monopoly in gas transport: one large line is always cheaper per unit than two small ones, so competing parallel pipelines are wasteful.

Where the wording is imprecise: the second bullet says costs per length are proportional to "diameter and capacity". Both cannot be true at once. If cost per length were proportional to capacity, and capacity grows as D^2.58, then cost per length would grow as D^2.58 as well and the third bullet - and the conclusion - would collapse. The correct statement, and the one the formula on slide 177 implements, is that cost per length is proportional to the diameter, and therefore proportional to capacity^(1/2.58), i.e. to about capacity^0.39. Read the bullet as "cost per length rises with diameter, and hence with capacity, but under-proportionally in capacity".

The 95 % figure carries the rest of the lecture: with almost all cost fixed, the specific transport cost is dictated by utilisation, marginal cost is close to zero, and average cost falls over the whole relevant output range - the textbook definition of a natural monopoly and the reason network tariffs must be regulated.

prompt: State the transportation principle and the profitability condition on this slide, and apply it: gas costs 28 EUR/MWh at Hub 1 and can be sold at 33 EUR/MWh at Hub 2. Is a transport at 3 EUR/MWh worthwhile? What if the transport costs 6 EUR/MWh, and what changes if the capacity has already been booked and 5 of those 6 EUR/MWh are the capacity charge?
solution:
The principle: the shipper buys gas at location 1 (Hub 1) at the price p_supply, injects it at A into the reserved transport capacity, has it transported at p_transport, withdraws it at B and sells it at location 2 (Hub 2) at p_sales. The condition for the intended business transaction to be profitable is

p_supply + p_transport < p_sales.

Case 1: 28 + 3 = 31 < 33. The condition holds; the transaction earns a margin of 33 - 31 = 2 EUR/MWh. The transport is worthwhile.

Case 2: 28 + 6 = 34 > 33. The condition fails by 1 EUR/MWh. The transaction destroys value and should not be done - the capacity stays unused, which is exactly how a transport tariff that is too high leaves physically available capacity idle and keeps two market areas apart. The maximum transport price the shipper can pay here is the locational spread itself, p_sales - p_supply = 5 EUR/MWh.

Case 3: capacity already booked, 5 of the 6 EUR/MWh being the capacity charge. Then the 5 EUR/MWh is sunk: it is due whether or not gas flows, so it must not enter the decision. The relevant comparison uses only the avoidable, variable part: 28 + 1 = 29 < 33, margin 4 EUR/MWh. The shipper should transport. The general rule is that the booking decision is taken on full cost, while the dispatch decision once the booking exists is taken on variable cost only - the same distinction as between long-run and short-run marginal cost in power generation.

That is also why a transporter can sell interruptible capacity cheaply and why secondary capacity markets exist: a shipper who cannot cover his full booking cost from the spread will still use or resell capacity as long as it covers its variable cost.

prompt: Explain how working gas volume, injection rate and withdrawal rate are related to one another.
solution:
The three parameters describe one storage facility and are booked separately, but they are physically coupled — they cannot be chosen independently.

Total gas storage capacity = cushion gas + working gas volume. The cushion gas stays in the reservoir permanently and maintains the pressure; only the working gas volume can actually be cycled. The injection rate and the withdrawal rate are the maximum flows in and out, quoted in m³/h or kWh/h.

The coupling runs through reservoir pressure. When the store is full the pressure is high, so the withdrawal rate is at its maximum while the injection rate is at its lowest — pushing more gas in against a high pressure needs ever more compression. As the store empties the picture reverses: injection becomes easy, withdrawal falls off. The rates are therefore not constant but a function of the filling level, which is why storage contracts quote them together with a curve or with the reservoir type.

Working gas volume divided by the withdrawal rate gives the number of hours or days of full withdrawal, and its inverse is the cycling rate. A large working gas volume with a small withdrawal rate is a seasonal store (typically a depleted field or an aquifer); a small working gas volume with a high withdrawal rate is a peak-shaving store (typically a salt cavern). More cushion gas buys a higher rate for the same working gas volume — that is the trade-off the operator sizes.
slide_title: Cushion gas working gas volume Working gas capacity total gas storage capacity

prompt: Is it profitable to buy natural gas at the summer price, store it and sell it in winter?
solution:
The storage principle slide gives the condition directly: p_supply + p_storage < p_sales. Buying, storing and selling only pays if the summer/winter spread exceeds the specific storage cost.

With the lecture's storage example the specific storage cost is 544,500 € / 132,000 MWh = 4.125 €/MWh. The summer/winter spread slide shows a winter price of 28 €/MWh against a summer price of 27 €/MWh, i.e. a spread of 1 €/MWh.

1 €/MWh < 4.125 €/MWh → the business makes a loss.
Revenue from the spread: 132,000 MWh · 1 €/MWh = 132,000 €
Storage cost: 544,500 €
Result: −412,500 € per year.

That is the point of the slide: the spread alone says nothing. Only spread minus storage cost decides, and in recent years the seasonal spread has often been too thin to pay for a storage booking — which is exactly why the merit order of German storages and the ambiguity of storage prices are discussed right afterwards. A trader who cannot earn the spread will prefer the time swap, which needs no physical capacity.

prompt: How high would the winter selling price have to be for the storage business to break even?
solution:
Rearrange the profitability condition p_supply + p_storage < p_sales to its break-even form:
p_sales = p_supply + p_storage

With the summer price of 27 €/MWh and the specific storage cost of 4.125 €/MWh:
p_sales = 27 + 4.125 = 31.125 €/MWh

The winter price would have to be at least 31.13 €/MWh, i.e. the summer/winter spread would have to reach 4.125 €/MWh instead of the 1 €/MWh shown on the slide. At the actual 28 €/MWh the trader loses 3.125 €/MWh, which over 132,000 MWh is the −412,500 € from the previous part.

General form: the break-even spread equals the specific storage cost, which itself is (p_injection·κ_inj + p_withdrawal·κ_wd + p_working gas·v_wg) divided by the working gas volume in MWh. Everything that raises the booked rates without raising the cycled volume pushes the break-even price up.

prompt: Name and explain the three functions of natural gas storage.
solution:
1. Compensation of demand fluctuations — short-term and mid-term. Gas demand is strongly temperature-correlated: households and heating consume several times more in January than in July, and within a day there are morning and evening peaks. Production and pipeline imports, by contrast, run close to a flat band because their capacity is expensive and wants high utilisation. Storage takes the difference: it is filled in summer and emptied in winter (seasonal, mid-term) and it covers the daily and hourly peaks (short-term, peak shaving).

2. Compensation of supply fluctuations. If a producing field, a pipeline or an LNG cargo fails, the storage steps in. This is the security-of-supply function that the EU and German storage laws turned into a legal filling obligation after 2022 — storage substitutes for supply that does not arrive.

3. (Economic) optimisation. Storage is also a trading asset. Gas is bought when it is cheap and sold when it is expensive; the condition is p_supply + p_storage < p_sales. On top of that the store can be re-optimised as prices move, which is where the option value of a storage booking comes from.

The three functions correspond to three different technical profiles: seasonal stores (depleted fields, aquifers — large working gas volume, low rates) serve function 1 and 2, salt caverns (small volume, high rates, several cycles per year) serve the peak and the trading function.

prompt: A trader reserves transport capacity under an entry-exit pricing system: 10,000 m³/h at the entry point for 2 €/kWh/h/a and the same capacity at the exit point for 0.01 €/kWh/h/day. The calorific value of the natural gas is 11 kWh/m³. How much does he pay for the reservation of transport capacity in one year?
solution:
Step 1 — convert the volumetric capacity into energy capacity:
κ_E = κ_V · GCV = 10,000 m³/h · 11 kWh/m³ = 110,000 kWh/h = 110,000 kW = 110 MW

Step 2 — entry point (price already per year):
110,000 kW · 2 €/kW/a = 220,000 €/a

Step 3 — exit point (price per day, so multiply by 365):
110,000 kW · 0.01 €/kW/day · 365 d/a = 401,500 €/a

Step 4 — total annual transport capacity cost:
220,000 + 401,500 = 621,500 €/a

The two things that decide this task: convert to energy before touching a price, and check the period of every price. Note that €/(kWh/h)/a and €/kW/a are the same unit — a capacity price, paid for the right to flow, regardless of how much gas actually flows.

prompt: The same trader wants to store the natural gas: withdrawal capacity 3,000 m³/h, injection capacity 3,000 m³/h, working gas capacity 12 million m³. Prices: working gas 0.003 €/kWh/a, withdrawal 2 €/kWh/h/a, injection 2.5 €/kWh/h/a; calorific value 11 kWh/m³. How much does he pay for reserving the storage capacity in one year?
solution:
T_storage = p_injection · κ_injection + p_withdrawal · κ_withdrawal + p_working gas · v_working gas

Step 1 — rates to energy:
Withdrawal: 3,000 m³/h · 11 kWh/m³ = 33,000 kWh/h = 33,000 kW
Injection: 3,000 m³/h · 11 kWh/m³ = 33,000 kWh/h = 33,000 kW

Step 2 — rate charges:
Withdrawal: 33,000 kW · 2 €/kW/a = 66,000 €/a
Injection: 33,000 kW · 2.5 €/kW/a = 82,500 €/a

Step 3 — working gas (a quantity, not a rate):
12,000,000 m³ · 11 kWh/m³ = 132,000,000 kWh
132,000,000 kWh · 0.003 €/kWh/a = 396,000 €/a

Step 4 — total annual storage cost:
66,000 + 82,500 + 396,000 = 544,500 €/a

Watch the unit of the third component: the working gas price is €/kWh/a, an energy price, while injection and withdrawal are €/kW/a, capacity prices. Mixing the two is the standard mistake in this task.

prompt: The same trader buys 40 million m³ of natural gas at a price of 20 €/MWh (calorific value 11 kWh/m³). How much does he pay in total for this quantity?
solution:
Step 1 — convert the volume into energy:
40,000,000 m³ · 11 kWh/m³ = 440,000,000 kWh = 440,000 MWh

Step 2 — multiply by the commodity price:
440,000 MWh · 20 €/MWh = 8,800,000 €

The commodity is by far the largest item — 8.8 million € against 621,500 € of transport and 544,500 € of storage. Keep the 440,000 MWh: it is the denominator of the next part.

prompt: Given the transport, storage and purchase costs above: how high are the trader's total specific procurement costs, including the price of the natural gas, in €/MWh?
solution:
Step 1 — add up all costs:
Gas purchase 8,800,000 € + transport 621,500 € + storage 544,500 € = 9,966,000 €

Step 2 — divide by the energy procured:
9,966,000 € / 440,000 MWh = 22.65 €/MWh

Breakdown, which is the more informative way to present it:
Gas 20.00 €/MWh
Transport 621,500 / 440,000 = 1.41 €/MWh
Storage 544,500 / 440,000 = 1.24 €/MWh
Total 22.65 €/MWh

The lesson of the whole example: infrastructure adds about 13 % on top of the commodity price here, and it is a fixed cost — the trader pays the 1,166,000 € of capacity charges whether or not he uses the booked capacity. The fewer MWh he actually moves, the higher his specific cost becomes, which is exactly why utilisation matters so much in network industries.

prompt: Withdrawal capacity, injection capacity and working gas capacity are given with their prices, together with the gross calorific value. What does it cost to store 12 million m³ of natural gas for one year?
solution:
Storage is billed as three separate reservations, added up (slide "Storage Pricing"):
T_storage = p_injection · κ_injection + p_withdrawal · κ_withdrawal + p_working gas · v_working gas

The trick is always the same: convert volume into energy with the gross calorific value first, because the prices are quoted per kWh.

Worked with the lecture's own figures (GCV = 11 kWh/m³, withdrawal and injection capacity 3,000 m³/h each, working gas 12 million m³; prices 2 €/kWh/h/a withdrawal, 2.5 €/kWh/h/a injection, 0.003 €/kWh/a working gas):

Working gas: 12,000,000 m³ · 11 kWh/m³ = 132,000,000 kWh = 132,000 MWh
 → 132,000,000 kWh · 0.003 €/kWh/a = 396,000 €/a
Withdrawal: 3,000 m³/h · 11 kWh/m³ = 33,000 kWh/h = 33,000 kW
 → 33,000 kW · 2 €/kW/a = 66,000 €/a
Injection: 33,000 kW · 2.5 €/kW/a = 82,500 €/a

Total storage cost = 396,000 + 66,000 + 82,500 = 544,500 €/a

Specific storage cost = 544,500 € / 132,000 MWh = 4.125 €/MWh. That number is the one you need for the follow-up questions.

Note the unit identity that the slides use throughout: €/(kWh/h)/a = €/kW/a — a capacity price, not an energy price.

prompt: Explain the "time swap" and, in that context, the intrinsic and the extrinsic value.
solution:
Time swap. The intended business is to buy gas at time 1 at p_supply and sell it at time 2 at p_sales — physically that would need a storage facility. A time swap replaces the store with two market transactions at the *same* hub: the trader sells at time 1 at p1 and buys back at time 2 at p2. The lecture's profitability condition is p_supply − p1 < p_sales − p2, and compared with reserving storage capacity the swap is worthwhile whenever p2 − p1 < p_storage. Typically p1 < p2, so the swap costs money — but it may still be cheaper than the storage fee, and it needs no physical asset.

Intrinsic value. The value a storage position can lock in today, risk-free, from the observable forward curve: buy the summer contract, sell the winter contract and hold the spread. It is simply the summer/winter spread minus the storage cost, capped by the injection and withdrawal rates. If the forward spread is smaller than the storage price, the intrinsic value is zero.

Extrinsic value. The additional, optional value that only materialises if prices move. A store is not obliged to follow one seasonal cycle: it can re-optimise, inject and withdraw repeatedly and thus monetise volatility. That optionality is worth something even when the intrinsic value is zero, and it grows with price volatility and with the cycling rate of the facility. Total storage value = intrinsic value + extrinsic value.
note: The slides show the time swap and the comparison with storage, but they never use the terms "intrinsic" and "extrinsic value" — that part of the question goes beyond the deck. The definitions above are the standard ones and are consistent with the summer/winter-spread slides.

prompt: Describe the two curves in the figure 'Storage Parameters' Interdependence' — what is on the axes, how does each curve run — and explain the physics behind them and the consequence for a storage contract.
solution:
The horizontal axis is the working gas volume currently in the store, i.e. the filling level; the vertical axis carries both rates.

The withdrawal rate (blue) starts very low at an almost empty store, rises steeply and then saturates at its maximum for a well-filled store. The injection rate (red) does the opposite: it is at its maximum while the store is fairly empty, stays flat for a long stretch and then falls away steeply as the store approaches full. The two curves cross at roughly half filling.

The physics is the reservoir pressure. A full store has high pressure, so gas flows out by itself and the withdrawal rate is at its maximum, whereas pushing further gas in against that pressure needs ever more compression power — the injection rate collapses. An empty store has low pressure, so injection is easy while withdrawal has too little driving pressure. This is also why the cushion gas exists: it is the pressure pad that keeps the withdrawal rate usable at low filling levels, and more cushion gas buys a higher rate for the same working gas volume.

Consequence for the contract: the three storage parameters cannot be chosen independently. A contract therefore does not quote one withdrawal rate but a rate curve or ratchet table as a function of the filling level, and the nominal rate is only guaranteed above a certain level. For the trader this means the store is least able to deliver exactly when it has already been drawn down — late in a cold winter — which is a security-of-supply issue and not only a commercial one.
slide_title: Injection rate Withdrawal rate Working gas volume

prompt: A storage facility is filled almost to its maximum working gas volume. According to the interdependence curves, which statement is correct?
options: The withdrawal rate is at its maximum and the injection rate has fallen to its minimum, because the reservoir pressure is high.
Both rates are at their maximum, because rates depend only on the compressor size and not on the filling level.
The injection rate is at its maximum and the withdrawal rate at its minimum, because the reservoir pressure is high.
Both rates fall, because the cushion gas can no longer maintain the pressure at a high filling level.
solution: At a high filling level the reservoir pressure is high. Gas therefore flows out easily — maximum withdrawal rate — while injecting further gas against that pressure needs increasing compression power, so the injection rate drops off. Option 1 reverses the two and describes the nearly empty store. Option 2 ignores the whole point of the slide: the rates are functions of the filling level, not constants. Option 3 misunderstands the cushion gas, whose job is to hold the pressure up at low filling levels, not at high ones.
