prompt: Write down the net present value formula as it is given on the slide, explain every symbol, and state which interest rate is used in practice and why.
solution:
NPV = sum over t = 0 to n of (Revenue_t - Expenditure_t) / (1+i)^t = sum over t = 0 to n of Cash Flow_t / (1+i)^t.

Symbols: t is the period, n is the lifetime of the project, i is the discount or interest rate, Revenue_t - Expenditure_t is the net cash flow of period t. In words: the net present value is the sum of the differences between the present values of all revenues and expenditures, i.e. the sum of the discounted cash flows.

The investment enters as a negative cash flow in the first periods (in the wind farm example even before t = 0, so those instalments have to be compounded rather than discounted, or the reference date has to be set at the first instalment). The rate used in practice is the WACC, the weighted average cost of capital: a project is financed by a mixture of equity and debt, and the WACC weights the required return on equity and the interest on debt by their shares. Discounting with the WACC means that a positive NPV is a surplus over and above the full remuneration of both capital providers.

prompt: Using the techno-economic data of the wind farm example (specific investment 1000 EUR/kW, installed capacity 100 MW, WACC 10 %, 30 % of the investment two years and 70 % one year before commissioning, feed-in tariff 8 EUR ct/kWh, 2000 full load hours per year, annual fixed O&M costs 2 % of the investment), set up the complete cash flow profile of the project. State every intermediate result and every unit conversion.
solution:
Investment: 100 MW = 100,000 kW; 100,000 kW x 1000 EUR/kW = 100 million EUR total. Split: 30 % = 30 million EUR two years before commissioning (2013 in the lecture chart) and 70 % = 70 million EUR one year before commissioning (2014).

Annual generation: 100 MW x 2000 h/a = 200,000 MWh/a = 200 GWh/a. The full load hours already contain the availability and the wind resource, so no further correction is applied.

Revenue: the tariff of 8 EUR ct/kWh is 80 EUR/MWh (1 ct/kWh = 10 EUR/MWh). Revenue = 200,000 MWh/a x 80 EUR/MWh = 16 million EUR/a, guaranteed and constant because it is a feed-in tariff, not a market price.

Fixed costs: 2 % of the investment = 0.02 x 100 million EUR = 2 million EUR/a for O&M.

Net annual cash flow = 16 - 2 = 14 million EUR/a, constant over the 20 operating years (2015-2034 in the lecture chart).

Cash flow profile: -30 million EUR in 2013, -70 million EUR in 2014, then +14 million EUR in each of the 20 years 2015 to 2034. This one profile is the input for all four dynamic methods that follow - NPV, annuity, IRR and discounted payback period.

prompt: With an installed capacity of 100 MW and 2000 full load hours per year the wind farm of the example produces ___ GWh of electricity per year.
solution: 100 MW x 2000 h/a = 200,000 MWh/a = 200 GWh/a. Full load hours are the equivalent number of hours at rated power; 2000 h/a corresponds to a capacity factor of 2000/8760 = 23 %, a typical value for onshore wind. At the feed-in tariff of 8 EUR ct/kWh = 80 EUR/MWh this generation yields 16 million EUR of revenue per year.

prompt: What does the annuity method add compared with the net present value method?
options: It adds non-financial criteria to the monetary evaluation

It transfers revenues and expenditures into a uniform series from t = 1 to n, so the result is an average yearly rather than a total profit; the recommendation itself is the same as with the NPV method
It uses a different interest rate, namely the internal rate of return instead of the WACC
It replaces discounting by a static average over the yearly cash flows
solution: The annuity method is based on the net present value method and gives the same recommendations; it only expresses the result differently. Revenues and expenditures that vary over time are first turned into a net present value and then spread over the lifetime as a uniform series (annuity) from t = 1 to n, so that average yearly expenditures and revenues can be compared and the alternative with the highest annuity is chosen. This is the natural form whenever a yearly figure is wanted (EUR per year, or divided by the annual generation, EUR/MWh as a levelised cost) and it is the only clean way to compare projects of different lifetimes.

prompt: Derive the capital recovery factor from the time line on the slide: how do you convert a present value C0 into a uniform series of n payments r, and what is the relation between CRF and PVA?
solution:
The time line shows C0 at t = 0 and then a payment r at the end of every period t = 1, 2, ..., n. Discounting the series gives

C0 = r(1+i)^-1 + r(1+i)^-2 + ... + r(1+i)^-n = r x [(1+i)^n - 1] / [(1+i)^n x i].

The bracket is the present value annuity factor PVA - the present value of one monetary unit per year for n years. Solving for r inverts it:

r = C0 x [(1+i)^n x i] / [(1+i)^n - 1] = C0 x CRF, with CRF = 1/PVA.

The capital recovery factor CRF is therefore the yearly payment that repays one unit of capital plus interest over n years - exactly the annuity of a loan. Two things to watch in the exam: the first payment falls at t = 1, one full period after the reference date C0, so a series that starts in 2015 has its reference date in 2014; and CRF > i always, because the annuity has to cover both the interest and the repayment, approaching i only for very large n.

prompt: Apply the annuity method to the wind farm example (investment 30 million EUR in 2013 and 70 million EUR in 2014, net cash flow 14 million EUR/a in 2015-2034, i = 10 %). Determine the annuity of the project and check the result against the NPV of 14.7 million EUR.
solution:
Step 1 - capital recovery factor for the 20 operating years: CRF(20; 10 %) = 0.1 x 1.1^20 / (1.1^20 - 1) = 0.1 x 6.7275 / 5.7275 = 0.1175. The table on slide 501 lists only t = 1...10 and t = 30, so for t = 20 the factor has to be computed from the formula.

Step 2 - value of the investment at the reference date. The 20 annuity payments run from 2015 to 2034, so their reference date is 2014, one year before the first payment. Compounding the instalments to 2014: 30 x 1.1 + 70 = 33 + 70 = 103.0 million EUR.

Step 3 - annuity of the capital cost: 103.0 x 0.1175 = 12.1 million EUR/a.

Step 4 - annuity of the project: the operating cash flow is already a uniform series of 14 million EUR/a, so the annuity of the project is 14 - 12.1 = 1.9 million EUR/a. It is positive, so the project is realised - the same recommendation as the NPV method gives.

Cross-check: discount the annuity back. 1.9 x PVA(20; 10 %) = 1.9 x 8.514 = 16.2 million EUR in 2014, and 16.2/1.1 = 14.7 million EUR in 2013 - exactly the NPV. Interpretation: the wind farm earns 14 million EUR a year, of which 12.1 million EUR are needed to service and repay the capital at 10 %; 1.9 million EUR a year are left over as a genuine surplus.

prompt: Reproduce the taxonomy of investment appraisal methods from the slide (the red circle marks the group treated in this lecture) and state the criterion that separates the two branches.
solution:
The tree starts at 'Investment Appraisal Methods' and splits into Static and Dynamic.

Static branch: single-period methods - Profit Comparison Method, Cost Comparison Method, Average Return Method - and multi-period methods, of which the slide names the Simple Payback Method.

Dynamic branch (the red circle, i.e. the subject of this chapter): Net Present Value (NPV) Method, Annuity Method, Internal Rate of Return Method and Discounted Payback Period.

The separating criterion is the treatment of time. Static methods compare one representative period or an average and simply add up amounts from different years; they ignore the time value of money. Dynamic methods discount every cash flow to a common reference date with (1+i)^t, so the timing of a payment changes its weight: an amount received in year 20 counts far less than the same amount received in year 1. The price of this is that dynamic methods need a complete cash flow profile over the whole lifetime and an interest rate, whereas a static method needs one typical year.
slide_title: Investment Appraisal Static and Dynamic methods of Investment appraisal

prompt: The internal rate of return (IRR) is the interest rate at which the net present value of an investment becomes exactly ___.
solution: Zero. The condition on the slide is: sum over t = 1 to n of (Revenue_t - Expenditure_t)/(1+i)^t - Investment = 0; the i that solves it is the internal rate of return, also called internal interest rate of return method or time-adjusted rate of return. Decision rule: choose the alternative with the highest internal interest rate, and realise a project only if its IRR exceeds the cost of capital. For n > 2 the equation is a polynomial of degree n in i and cannot be solved in closed form, which is why the following slide offers simulation, a graphical solution or an approximation procedure such as Newton's method. The great advantage of the IRR is that it is a percentage and therefore independent of the project size; that is also its weakness, because a large project with a lower IRR can create far more value than a small one with a high IRR.

prompt: Determine the discounted payback period of the wind farm from the chart and reproduce the calculation. How many years of operation are needed, and why is the discounted payback period so much longer than the simple one?
solution:
The cumulated discounted cash flow starts at -30 million EUR (2013), falls to its minimum of -93.6 million EUR (2014) and then rises. It crosses the zero line in 2028, which is the year highlighted on the slide. So the discounted payback period ends in 2028: 14 years of operation (2015-2028), or 16 years after the first instalment.

Calculation: the discounted cash flow of year t is 14/1.1^t with t counted from 2013, i.e. 11.57 (2015), 10.52 (2016), 9.56, 8.69, 7.90, 7.18, 6.53, 5.94, 5.40, 4.91, 4.46, 4.05, 3.69 (2027) and 3.35 (2028) million EUR. Cumulating them against the 93.64 million EUR present value of the investment leaves -3.2 million EUR after 2027; the 3.35 million EUR of 2028 push the balance to about +0.1 million EUR. That is the payback point.

Comparison: undiscounted, the 100 million EUR investment is recovered by 14 million EUR/a in 100/14 = 7.1 years of operation. Discounting more than doubles this, because the later a cash flow lies the less it contributes - 14 million EUR in 2034 are worth only 1.9 million EUR in 2013 at 10 %. The remaining six years after the payback point (2029-2034) contribute the whole NPV of 14.7 million EUR, which shows why the DPP alone would be a poor decision criterion.

prompt: Which limitation of investment appraisal does slide 511 ('Limitations 2/2') state?
options: The methods require probabilities for all states of nature, which are usually unknown
The methods cannot handle projects with a lifetime of more than 30 years
It is difficult or impossible in practice to assign a proportionate revenue or investment to a single investment, and non-financial and qualitative factors are not considered at all
Discounting is mathematically undefined for negative cash flows
solution: The attribution problem is the first point of the slide: in an integrated system a new plant, a grid reinforcement or an IT system changes the result of the whole portfolio, and cutting out 'its' revenue is largely arbitrary. Added to that, every investment carries a risk, for which the lecture proposes scenario planning techniques, and non-financial and qualitative factors (acceptance, strategy, know-how, security of supply) do not appear in the cash flow at all. The conclusion of the slide: an investment decision must not be reached by investment appraisal methods alone, investment decisions are entrepreneurial decisions; multi-criteria approaches can support the decision process, but no method is intended to replace the decision makers. Option 3 is wrong because probabilities are exactly what the dynamic methods do not need - that is the subject of the next chapter.

prompt: Sketch the matrix on the slide and locate the entrepreneurial perspective, the governmental perspective and strategic decision making in energy systems in it.
solution:
The matrix has three columns - Certainty, Risk, Uncertainty - and two rows: 'one decision criterion (e.g. payoff, NPV...)' and 'multiple decision criteria (e.g. economic, ecological, sociological criteria)'.

Three ellipses are drawn over it. A horizontal ellipse on the upper row, reaching into the uncertainty column, is labelled entrepreneurial perspective: a company decides on one monetary criterion, the payoff or the NPV. A second horizontal ellipse on the lower row, again reaching into the uncertainty column, is labelled governmental perspective: the state weighs economic, ecological and social criteria simultaneously. A vertical ellipse encloses the whole uncertainty column and is labelled strategic decision making in energy systems.

The message: strategic decisions in the energy sector always sit in the uncertainty column - neither certainty nor known probabilities are available for the relevant horizons. What distinguishes the company from the state is not the environment but the number of criteria. This is exactly the structure of the chapter: first the one-criterion rules under uncertainty (maximax, maximin, minimax regret, Laplace, Hurwicz), then multi-criteria approaches with stakeholder involvement.
slide_title: Types Of Decision Making Environments (2) Certainty Risk Uncertainty

prompt: The payoff table of the lecture example (profits in EUR 1000) is: d1, an investment in a coal-fired power plant, yields 20 in s1 and 6 in s2; d2, an investment in a CCGT, yields 25 in s1 and 3 in s2. Apply all five decision rules and state which alternative each of them selects.
solution:
Maximax (optimistic): the row maxima are 20 for d1 and 25 for d2; the largest single value in the table is 25, so choose d2.

Maximin (conservative): the row minima are 6 for d1 and 3 for d2; the maximum of these minima is 6, so choose d1.

Minimax regret: the column maxima are 25 in s1 and 6 in s2. Regret table: d1 gets 25-20 = 5 and 6-6 = 0, maximum regret 5; d2 gets 25-25 = 0 and 6-3 = 3, maximum regret 3. The minimum of the maximum regrets is 3, so choose d2.

Laplace (equally likely): average for d1 = (20+6)/2 = 13, average for d2 = (25+3)/2 = 14, so choose d2.

Hurwicz with a coefficient of risk attitude a = 0.8: payoff for d1 = 0.8 x 20 + 0.2 x 6 = 17.2, payoff for d2 = 0.8 x 25 + 0.2 x 3 = 20.6, so choose d2.

Four of the five rules select d2, only the conservative maximin selects d1. That is the didactic point of the example: with the same data the recommendation depends on the rule, i.e. on the risk attitude of the decision maker, not on the facts. d2 has both the better best case (25 against 20) and the worse worst case (3 against 6) - it is the riskier alternative, and every rule that puts weight on the good outcomes picks it.

prompt: An investor compares three projects - d1 a hard coal plant, d2 a CCGT and d3 a wind farm - under three scenarios. The payoff table gives the NPV in million EUR: d1: 40 (s1), 15 (s2), -10 (s3); d2: 30, 25, 5; d3: 10, 20, 22. Apply the maximax rule. Which project is chosen, and what does the choice reveal about the decision maker?
solution:
Maximax means: list the maximum payoff of every decision and choose the largest of them.

Row maxima: d1 = 40 (in s1), d2 = 30 (in s1), d3 = 22 (in s3). The largest single value in the table is 40, so the maximax rule selects d1, the hard coal plant.

What the choice reveals: the decision maker is an optimist who evaluates each alternative solely by its best case and behaves as if the favourable scenario s1 would occur. The rule uses exactly one of the nine numbers in the table and therefore ignores that d1 is the only alternative with a loss - it destroys 10 million EUR of value in s3, the worst outcome in the whole table - and that its result in the middle scenario, 15, is the weakest of the three. A single optimistic estimate in one cell can drive the whole decision, which is why the lecture calls maximax and maximin of limited benefit in reality. In an exam always add this qualification instead of only naming the winner.

prompt: From the entrepreneurial perspective, what happens to an investment appraisal once it is combined with a set of scenarios, and which two central challenges does the lecture derive from this?
solution:
The main target of energy systems analysis is to generate a set of scenarios as a framework for analysing the chances and risks of strategic decisions. The consequence for the appraisal is that an investment decision is no longer represented by one figure but by a bandwidth of NPVs - one for each scenario. It is likely that a project achieves a positive NPV in one scenario and a negative NPV in another, and the same holds for every other indicator, e.g. the IRR or the discounted payback period.

From this the lecture derives two central challenges. First, communication: how can the uncertainties, i.e. the chances and risks associated with the investment decision, be transported, communicated and visualised to the decision makers in an understandable way? A board does not decide on a distribution, it decides on a project, so the bandwidth has to be made readable - which is what the visualisation with present values of capex, opex and gross margins per scenario is for. Second, interpretation: how can and should the information on the uncertainties be used in the decision-making process, i.e. how should the results be interpreted? This is exactly the question the decision rules under uncertainty - maximax, maximin, minimax regret, Laplace and Hurwicz - try to answer by condensing the bandwidth into one number.
slide_title: Decision making in the energy sector The entrepreneurial perspective

prompt: A CCGT plant generates 500 MW. It can be connected to the grid either with a 110 kV or with a 380 kV line; the resistance is 6 Ω. Calculate the power loss Pv for both cases.
solution:
The lecture works with P = U · I and Pv = I² · R.

110 kV line:
I = P / U = 500 · 10^6 W / (110 · 10^3 V) = 4,545 A
Pv = I² · R = (4,545 A)² · 6 Ω = 1.24 · 10^8 W ≈ 124 MW
That is about 24.8 % of the transmitted 500 MW.

380 kV line:
I = P / U = 500 · 10^6 W / (380 · 10^3 V) = 1,316 A
Pv = I² · R = (1,316 A)² · 6 Ω = 1.04 · 10^7 W ≈ 10.4 MW
That is about 2.1 % of the transmitted 500 MW.

Both steps collapse into Pv = R · P² / U², which shows the mechanism directly: losses fall with the square of the voltage. Going from 110 kV to 380 kV reduces them by a factor of (380/110)² ≈ 11.9. Conclusion, exactly as on the slide: reduce resistance, reduce current, raise the voltage by transforming — which is why long-distance transmission uses the extra-high-voltage level.
note: The lecture uses the single-phase relation P = U · I. With the correct three-phase relation I = P/(√3·U·cos φ) and Pv = 3·I²·R you arrive at the same Pv = R·P²/U², so the numbers are unaffected — but write down the formula the lecture uses.

prompt: Name the four types of control reserve in the electricity system and state who is responsible for each.
solution:
Electrical energy cannot be stored to any relevant extent, so feed-in and withdrawal have to match permanently. Any imbalance shows up immediately as a frequency deviation from the 50 Hz target (tolerance band 49.95–50.05 Hz), caused by unforeseeable events — generation failures, grid disruptions — and by forecast inaccuracies, which grow with the share of stochastic wind and PV. Control reserve is graded by how fast it has to be there:

1. Primary control — activated within seconds, fully available after 30 s. Stabilises the frequency; delivered by all connected generators jointly.
2. Secondary control — takes over from about 30 s and is fully available after some minutes up to 15 min. Restores the frequency to 50 Hz and returns the primary reserve.
3. Tertiary control / minute reserve — from 15 min up to about 1 h. Relieves the secondary reserve and covers longer disturbances.
4. Hourly reserve — everything beyond one hour.

Responsibility: the transmission system operator procures and calls the first three. From one hour onwards the balancing group manager has to restore its own balance, i.e. responsibility passes from the TSO to the balancing group. Further system services outside this ladder are reactive power compensation and black start capability.
note: The slide labels the second band "Primary control" a second time — the German text layer underneath it reads "Sekundärregelung", so it is the secondary control band. Read the diagram along the time axis (5 s / 30 s / 15 min / 1 h) rather than by the English labels.

prompt: Describe how a single-phase alternating voltage is generated according to the slide, name the three labelled parts of the machine, and give the equations for u(t), i(t) and the angular frequency. What is the angular frequency at 50 Hz?
solution:
A conductor loop rotates in the constant magnetic field between the north and the south pole of a magnet. The flux linked with the loop changes with the rotation angle, so a voltage is induced; it is tapped from the rotating loop through two slip rings and the carbon brushes sliding on them. The three labels on the drawing are conductor loop, slip rings and carbon brushes.

Because the induced voltage is proportional to the rate of change of the flux, which varies sinusoidally with the angle, one gets
u(t) = u_max x sin(wt), i(t) = i_max x sin(wt), with w = 2 pi f.

The slide shows the same process in two representations. In the pointer diagram (phasor diagram) a pointer of length equal to the amplitude rotates counter-clockwise; its projection on the vertical axis is the instantaneous value. In the line chart to the right of it that projection is plotted over the angle from 0 to 360 degrees, which produces the sine curve; the two are linked by horizontal construction lines at 30, 60, 90 degrees and so on. One full revolution of the pointer corresponds to one period T of the sine.

At f = 50 Hz the angular frequency is w = 2 pi x 50 = 314 per second, and one period lasts T = 1/f = 20 ms. Note that for a purely ohmic load current and voltage are written with the same argument, i.e. they are in phase; a phase shift appears only with reactive components, which is the subject of the next slides.

prompt: The slide shows the curves of voltage, current and power for a purely ohmic load. Give the equation for the instantaneous power, explain why the power curve never becomes negative, and say what that means physically.
solution:
The instantaneous power is the product of the instantaneous values:
P = U_max x sin(wt) x I_max x sin(wt - phi).

With a purely ohmic (effective) resistance R there is no phase shift between current and voltage, so phi = 0 and P = U_max x I_max x sin(wt) squared. A squared sine is never negative: the power curve lies entirely in the positive range, touching zero at the zero crossings of u and i and reaching U_max x I_max at their peaks. It oscillates at twice the frequency of voltage and current - with alternating current the power, like the current and the voltage, constantly oscillates between a maximum and a minimum.

Physically this means that the resistance absorbs electrical power at every moment and releases it, for example as heat; no energy ever flows back to the source. The average of the curve is U_max x I_max / 2 = U_eff x I_eff, and this average is the active power P, the only part that does useful work. This is the reference case: as soon as an inductive or capacitive component is added, current and voltage drift apart, part of the power curve falls below the time axis, and the average - the active power - becomes smaller than the product of the effective values.

prompt: Why does the power system need system services at all? Name the physical reason, the tolerance band that has to be kept, the causes of imbalance and two system services besides control reserve.
solution: The physical reason is that electrical energy cannot be stored to any significant extent. Feed-in and withdrawal must therefore balance permanently and at every instant; any imbalance appears immediately as a deviation of the system frequency from its target value of 50 Hz. The permitted tolerance band is 49.95 to 50.05 Hz - too much generation pushes the frequency up, too little pulls it down. Two groups of causes disturb the balance: unforeseeable events such as generation failures and grid disruptions, and forecast inaccuracies, which grow with the increasing use of stochastic energy sources, especially wind. Besides the control reserve ladder, the transmission system operators procure further system services: reactive power compensation, which keeps the voltage within its limits, and black start capability, i.e. units that can be started without any external supply to rebuild the grid after a blackout.

prompt: In the control-reserve diagram, the band that takes over from about 30 s and is fully available after up to 15 min is the ___ control band.
solution: Secondary control (Sekundärregelung). It relieves the primary control from about 30 s onwards, brings the frequency back to exactly 50 Hz and frees the primary reserve again, so it is fully available after a few minutes up to 15 min. Careful with this figure: the English label printed on the second band reads 'Primary control' a second time, which is a mistake in the slide - the German text layer underneath it says 'Sekundärregelung', and the German layer under the third band says 'Minutenreserve' for the tertiary control. Read the diagram along the time axis (5 s / 30 s / 15 min / 1 h) rather than by the English labels.

prompt: Sketch the path of electrical energy from the power plant to the household and name the voltage of every stage.
solution: The chain has four stages: generation - transport - distribution - customer. Generators in large power plants produce at 6-21 kV; a machine transformer steps this up immediately, because transport at generator voltage would be impossible in terms of losses. Transport happens in the extra-high-voltage transmission network at 380, 220 kV, which carries the energy over long distances and connects the control areas with each other. Distribution then works downwards in three steps: the high voltage network (110 kV) supplies regions and large industry, the medium voltage network (e.g. 20, 10 kV) supplies districts, industrial estates and rail, and the low voltage level (400 V) delivers the final energy to the customer. Every step down is a transformer, and every transformer costs efficiency - which is why the German transport and transformation losses add up to about 4.7 %.

prompt: The slide shows the German extra-high-voltage network twice, once as of 01.01.2003 and once as of 01.01.2020. Which line classes does the legend distinguish, and which two structural changes are visible between the two maps?
solution: The legend distinguishes the lines by operating voltage and by current type: 380 kV alternating-current lines (red in the 2003 map, orange in the 2020 map), 220 kV alternating-current lines (green) and HVDC overhead lines and cables (magenta), together with the substations and the converter stations. Two changes are visible. First, the network has been shifted upwards in voltage: many corridors that were 220 kV in 2003 carry 380 kV in 2020, because at the same transmitted power a higher voltage means a smaller current and the ohmic losses fall with the square of the current. Second, the 2020 map contains offshore connections in the North Sea and the Baltic Sea and a whole set of HVDC links under construction or in planning that run from north to south - the grid answer to wind generation in the north and to load plus closing nuclear plants in the south. Note the mismatch on the slide: the heading says Electricity exchange in Europe, but both maps show only the German transmission grid; the European dimension follows on the UCTE slides.

prompt: Explain with the help of the load curve how a pumped storage plant works economically, and what it does to the merit order.
solution: The figure shows a daily load curve over 24 hours and, on the right, the merit-order blocks 1 to 6 stacked by increasing marginal cost. In the night valley the plant runs in pumping operation: it adds artificial load, so the residual load curve is lifted, and the additional energy is supplied by the cheap base-load blocks 1 to 3 that are running anyway. At the midday peak the plant runs in turbine operation: it feeds back and shaves the peak, so the expensive peak-load blocks 5 and 6 are no longer needed. Comparing the load curve without pumped storage operation with the load curve with pumped storage operation, the pumped storage plant flattens the curve from both ends - it fills the valleys and shaves the peaks. The business case is exactly this price spread: buy cheap base-load energy at night, sell expensive peak energy at noon, and earn the difference minus the round-trip losses (a pumped storage plant returns roughly 75-80 % of the electricity it took in). The example on the slide is the Waldeck plant of E.ON.

prompt: Read the curtailment figures off the chart and explain why they are used as the argument for smart infrastructures.
solution: The chart gives the curtailed renewable energy in Germany in GWh: total curtailment rises from 74 GWh in 2009 over 421 GWh (2011) and 555 GWh (2013) to 1,581 GWh in 2014 and 4,722 GWh in 2015 - a factor of more than 60 in six years. Almost all of it is curtailed wind onshore (4,110 of the 4,722 GWh in 2015), and the striking line is the regional one: 3,055 GWh, about two thirds of the German total, are curtailed in Schleswig-Holstein alone. That is the argument: the energy is physically there, and it is thrown away not because of a lack of demand but because the grid between the windy north and the consuming south cannot transport it. The three ways out are grid expansion, storage, and making the system smart - shifting demand to the wind, or converting the surplus into hydrogen (power-to-X) instead of switching the turbines off. In more recent years the German curtailment has settled at roughly 6 TWh per year.

prompt: Draw the power-to-gas chain and label its steps.
solution:
Sketch the chain from left to right:

Renewable electricity (wind, PV, surplus generation) → electrolyser → hydrogen → (optional) methanation → SNG → gas infrastructure → end use, with an optional return path to power.

1. Electrolysis splits water: 2 H2O → 2 H2 + O2. The lecture's figures: alkaline about 4.7 kWh/Nm³ (≈ 64 % efficiency), SOEC about 3.6 kWh/Nm³ (≈ 83 %); PEM sits in between.
2. The hydrogen can be used directly — fed into a hydrogen network or a re-used natural gas pipeline, stored in salt caverns, or consumed in industry and mobility.
3. Or it is methanated with a CO2 stream from a point source or direct air capture to synthetic natural gas (SNG). The advantage the lecture stresses: SNG re-uses the *complete* existing natural gas infrastructure — pipelines, roughly 260 TWh of storage, power plants, heating systems, ships.
4. Re-electrification in a gas turbine, CCGT or fuel cell closes the loop to power-to-gas-to-power.

Mark the losses at every arrow — that is what the examiner is looking for.
note: The WS 25/26 decks no longer contain a dedicated power-to-gas slide. The chain has to be assembled from the electrolysis slide, the natural-gas-infrastructure-re-use slide and the synthetic methane slides.

prompt: How much hydrogen is consumed worldwide today, and roughly how much will be consumed around the middle of the century?
solution:
Today: global hydrogen production and consumption is about 110 Mt per year, of which renewable hydrogen is less than 1 % — roughly 0.09 Mt/a. It is almost entirely used as a chemical feedstock, not as an energy carrier: ammonia and fertiliser production takes about 45 % of it, refining most of the rest, plus methanol and steel.

2050: the projections in the lecture run in the range of roughly 500–700 Mt per year, i.e. a five- to sixfold increase, with the new demand coming from sectors that do not use hydrogen today — steel via direct reduction, shipping and aviation fuels, high-temperature industrial heat and some power generation.

Two caveats the lecture insists on. First, the projections diverge enormously between sources and have been revised downwards repeatedly — the slide on the uncertainty in global hydrogen trade projections is there for exactly that reason. Second, the clean hydrogen ladder ranks the applications: hydrogen is unavoidable for fertiliser, refining and steel, and a poor choice for domestic heating and passenger cars, where direct electrification wins.
note: Give the 110 Mt/a and the < 1 % renewable share as the hard numbers — those are printed on the slide. The 2050 figure depends on the source shown (IEA, IRENA, Hydrogen Council), so quote it as a range and say which scenario you mean.

prompt: How much electrolyser capacity is installed worldwide, and how much would be needed?
solution:
Installed: about 2 GW of electrolysis capacity worldwide by the end of 2024, with almost 5 GW expected by the end of 2025.

Needed: about 5,000 GW by 2050 — three orders of magnitude more than what stands today.

Put next to the 110 Mt/a of hydrogen produced today of which less than 1 % is renewable, this is the central reality check of the whole lecture: the announced projects and the physical build-out are far apart. The European roadmap on the following slide makes the same point in phases — phase 1 (2020–2024) 6 GW and more than 1 Mt/a, phase 2 (2025–2030) 40 GW and more than 10 Mt/a plus more than 10 Mt/a of imports.

If you are asked for one sentence: roughly 2 GW installed against roughly 5,000 GW required, so today's capacity is about 0.04 % of what the 2050 scenarios assume.

prompt: Which challenges does power-to-gas face in the context of the energy transition?
solution:
Efficiency. Every conversion costs: electrolysis 64–83 %, methanation again, re-electrification 40–60 %. The round trip therefore ends well below 40 %, so power-to-gas competes badly with direct electrification wherever direct use is possible — the clean hydrogen ladder puts it near the bottom for heating and cars.

Cost and full-load hours. Green hydrogen only becomes cheap with low electricity prices, but a plant that runs only on surplus power has too few full-load hours to earn back its capex. That is the central economic contradiction of the concept.

CO2 supply. Methanation needs a carbon source. Point sources are cheap but fossil, direct air capture is climate-neutral but expensive and energy-intensive.

Infrastructure. Hydrogen embrittles steel, so existing pipelines tolerate only limited blending; appliances, turbines and meters need adaptation. Re-use of the natural gas infrastructure is possible but not free. Volumetric energy density is low, storage needs caverns, and there is no liquid market or reliable pricing yet.

Water and siting. About 9 kg of water per kg of hydrogen, roughly 18 kg including cooling — a hard constraint in exactly the sunny, windy regions that are attractive for production.

Regulation and financing. Who pays for the hydrogen backbone, how is green hydrogen certified, and which subsidies bridge the gap until the technology is competitive.
slide_title: Challenges for Hydrogen as an Energy Carrier

prompt: What is hydrogen used for today, which reaction stands behind the largest single use, and why is this demand grey? Name the new demand segments the slide expects.
solution: Today hydrogen is almost entirely an industrial feedstock and not an energy carrier. The largest single use is ammonia and fertiliser production via the Haber-Bosch synthesis, N2 + 3 H2 -> 2 NH3; the second large use is refining, where hydrogen is needed for hydrocracking, denitrification and desulfurization. Both take their hydrogen almost exclusively from steam methane reforming of natural gas or from coal gasification, i.e. it is grey or brown hydrogen, which is why today's production already carries about 9.6 kg CO2 per kg H2. The upcoming segments are different in kind: industry (steel via direct reduced iron DRI, process heat above 1,000 °C, chemicals), transportation (heavy-duty trucks, shipping, aviation) and the power sector (flexible generation in turbines and fuel cells, large-scale energy storage).

prompt: The bar chart shows global hydrogen demand growing from 90 Mt in 2020 to 660 Mt in 2050, a factor of 7.5. Which statement about this projection is correct?
options: The chart is drawn in TWh, so the 660 for 2050 has to be read as TWh and not as million tons.
The growth is carried almost entirely by the existing industrial uses, which expand from 90 Mt to about 500 Mt.
Existing industry use stays roughly at today's level; the growth comes from new industry feedstock, building and industry heat, transport and power generation.
Demand already reaches 385 Mt in 2030, so the bulk of the growth happens in the current decade.
solution: Correct is the second option: the existing industry use, the light blue block containing refining and ammonia, stays roughly at today's order of magnitude of about 90 Mt, and the whole growth to 660 Mt comes from the new segments - new industry feedstock, building and industry heat, transport and power generation. The chart is labelled in million tons, not TWh. The intermediate values are 140 Mt in 2030 and 385 Mt in 2040, so the bulk of the growth falls into the 2030s and 2040s and not into the current decade.

prompt: The IEA figure splits hydrogen demand into unabated and low-emissions and gives the hydrogen share of four sub-sectors. Describe the two movements in the left panel up to 2050 and name the sub-sectors with the highest shares in the right panel.
solution: The left panel is drawn in EJ. Unabated hydrogen, i.e. hydrogen from unabated fossil sources, stands at about 11 to 12 EJ in 2024, mostly industry and refining, and shrinks steadily to roughly 3 EJ in 2050. Low-emissions hydrogen starts from almost nothing in 2024, reaches about 12 EJ in 2035 and about 38 EJ in 2050. The picture is therefore a double movement: the existing grey demand is substituted, and on top of it a much larger new demand is added, dominated by industry and transport in the Net Zero Emissions scenario. In the right panel shipping has the highest share of hydrogen and hydrogen-based fuels in 2050 at more than 50 %, mostly as ammonia, followed by aviation with roughly 40 %, almost entirely as synthetic hydrocarbon fuels, then steel with about 25 % and chemicals with about 14 %. The message is that hydrogen appears in the transport sub-sectors mainly through its derivatives, not as the pure molecule.

prompt: The figure gives the tolerance of existing elements of the natural gas network to hydrogen blending by volume. Which elements limit the achievable blend share, and what does that mean for a blending strategy?
solution: The tolerances differ by an order of magnitude. On the network side the distribution grid tolerates about 50 % by volume and up to 100 % under certain circumstances, gas meters about 50 %, the transmission grid about 20 %, compressors about 10 % and underground storage only about 2 %. On the end-use side boilers and cooking appliances tolerate about 30 %, CNG tanks about 30 % under certain circumstances, engines about 5 % and gas turbines about 2 %. The system limit is set by the weakest element actually present in the chain, i.e. underground storage and gas turbines at about 2 %, followed by engines and compressors. A blending strategy must therefore either stay at a very low single-digit share system-wide or be organised locally, since a distribution island with no storage and no turbine behind it can go far higher. Blending is also thermodynamically unattractive: hydrogen has only about a third of the volumetric energy content of methane, so 20 % hydrogen by volume replaces only about 7 % of the energy and saves correspondingly little CO2. The real answer is a dedicated hydrogen network, i.e. repurposing whole strings instead of blending into them.

prompt: Which two elements of the existing gas system tolerate the lowest hydrogen blend share according to the figure?
options: Boilers and cooking appliances, at about 30 %
Transmission pipelines and CNG tanks, at about 20 %
Distribution grid and gas meters, at about 50 %
Underground storage and gas turbines, at about 2 %
solution: Underground storage and gas turbines are the bottlenecks at roughly 2 % by volume - the storage because of microbiology, gas losses and reservoir chemistry, the turbines because of flame speed, flashback and NOx formation. Distribution and gas meters are the most tolerant network elements at about 50 %, boilers and cooking appliances lie around 30 %, and transmission pipelines are around 20 % with the compressors at about 10 %.

prompt: Slide 618 puts two maps of Europe side by side: the geological salt formations suitable for salt caverns, and the existing underground natural gas storages. Describe what each map shows and explain what the comparison tells you about where hydrogen storage can be built.
solution:
The left map shows the geological salt formations in Europe that could host salt cavern storages: a large belt running from the Netherlands and northern Germany across Poland, a second body over the North Sea and the UK, one further east towards Russia, and smaller lenses in France, Spain, Portugal and the Alpine region.

The right map plots the existing underground natural gas storages in Europe with three symbols: depleted fields (red stars), salt caverns (green diamonds) and aquifers (yellow squares). Depleted fields dominate by number and are spread all over Europe, while the salt caverns cluster exactly where the salt belt is: northern Germany, the Netherlands, Denmark, the UK and Poland.

The comparison matters because only salt caverns are today regarded as proven for hydrogen. Salt is practically impermeable, chemically inert, contains no residual hydrocarbons and no micro-organisms, and a cavern allows fast cycling with several turnovers per year. Porous formations, i.e. depleted fields and aquifers, carry the risk of hydrogen loss by diffusion through the cap rock, of reactions with the mineral matrix, and of microbial conversion of hydrogen into methane or hydrogen sulphide, so their hydrogen suitability is not yet proven.

Storage siting is therefore geologically fixed: hydrogen caverns can only be built on the salt belt, whereas Southern and South-Eastern Europe, which today store gas in depleted fields and aquifers, would have to rely on porous formations, on above-ground tanks or on pipeline imports from the north.

prompt: The right-hand map on slide 618 uses three symbols for the existing underground gas storages in Europe. Which statement about these three storage types is correct with respect to hydrogen?
options: Salt caverns are the type whose conversion to hydrogen is regarded as feasible; depleted fields and aquifers are porous formations whose hydrogen suitability is not yet proven.
Aquifers are the type with proven hydrogen suitability, because the water seal prevents any diffusion.
All three types can be converted to hydrogen without restriction; the only difference is the working gas volume.
Depleted gas fields are the preferred hydrogen option, because the existing wells and the residual gas can be re-used directly.
solution: The second option is correct. Salt caverns are leached into an impermeable, chemically inert and sterile rock salt body; conversion to hydrogen is regarded as feasible, at the price of losing about 80 % of the natural gas working capacity. Depleted fields and aquifers are porous formations: the hydrogen has to sit in the pore space of a sandstone under a cap rock, where it can diffuse, react with minerals and, above all, be eaten by sulphate-reducing and methanogenic bacteria that turn it into hydrogen sulphide or methane. That is why the lecture states 94 TWh of porous storage with hydrogen suitability not yet proven, against 168 TWh of salt cavern storage with conversion feasible. Residual hydrocarbons in a depleted field are a contamination problem, not an advantage, so option 3 is wrong as well.

prompt: The European Hydrogen Strategy of 2020 sets for phase 2 (2025-2030) 40 GW of electrolysis capacity, more than 10 Mt/a of production and more than 10 Mt/a of imports. Why does the strategy plan for as much import as domestic production, and what is phase 3 about?
solution:
Because Europe cannot produce cheap hydrogen at the volume it needs. Electricity is the dominant cost of electrolytic hydrogen, roughly 50 kWh_el per kg, so the hydrogen price follows the local full-load hours and the LCOE of wind and solar. In North Africa, the Middle East, Chile or Australia the same electrolyser runs far more hours per year on cheaper renewable electricity, which is why the fossil-fuel exporters are all building export projects. On top of that, land, grid connections and permits for the required renewable capacity are scarce in Europe, and after the loss of Russian pipeline gas the EU wants to diversify its supply rather than replace one dependency with another.

The strategy therefore doubles the volume by importing: 40 GW of electrolysis inside the EU plus 40 GW in the neighbourhood, giving more than 10 Mt/a of domestic production and more than 10 Mt/a of imports by 2030.

Phase 1 (2020-2024) was the pilot phase, 6 GW of electrolysis and more than 1 Mt/a of production. Phase 3 (2030-2050) contains no capacity target at all: hydrogen technologies should reach maturity so that hydrogen can decarbonise all sectors, in particular those that cannot be electrified directly (steel, chemicals, aviation, shipping, dispatchable power).

Reality check: phase 1 was missed by a wide margin, with only about 2 GW of electrolysis installed worldwide by the end of 2024 against 6 GW planned for the EU alone.

prompt: Name and quantify the challenges that make hydrogen difficult as an energy carrier, as slide 634 lists them.
solution:
Five challenges, four of them with hard numbers.

1. Low volumetric energy density. Compressed to 700 bar hydrogen holds only 1.3 kWh/l, and as a cryogenic liquid 2.4 kWh/l, against roughly 9.7 kWh/l for diesel. Per kilogram hydrogen is unbeatable at 33.33 kWh/kg; per litre it is poor, and transport and storage are volume problems, not mass problems.

2. Very low boiling point of -253 °C. Liquefaction for storage and shipping costs 10 - 14 kWh per kg of hydrogen today, about one third of the energy content of the hydrogen itself. The future expectation is about 7 kWh/kgH2 and the theoretical minimum is 2.9 kWh/kgH2. Liquid hydrogen also boils off continuously, about 0.2 % per day.

3. Highly flammable, with a very wide ignition range and a very low ignition energy, which is a safety problem especially in enclosed spaces and drives the cost of sensors, ventilation and clearance distances.

4. No existing infrastructure. Elements of the natural gas infrastructure can potentially be re-used - pipelines, salt caverns, terminals - but compressors, seals, meters, valves and burners have to be replaced or adapted, and steel embrittlement limits which lines can be converted.

5. Water demand, which is an export issue. Producing one kilogram of hydrogen consumes about 9 kg of water stoichiometrically, and about 18 kgH2O/kgH2 once cooling and demineralisation are included. Since the best solar and wind resources are in arid regions, export projects such as Coega or NEOM have to build seawater desalination as part of the plant.

prompt: Producing one kilogram of hydrogen by electrolysis requires about ___ kg of water stoichiometrically, and roughly twice that once cooling is included.
solution: About 9 kg of water per kg of hydrogen; the exact stoichiometric value from 2 H2O -> 2 H2 + O2 is 8.94 kg, as calculated in Exercise 1c. Including cooling and water treatment the figure roughly doubles to about 18 kgH2O/kgH2. This is a siting constraint rather than a global resource constraint: 9 kg of water per kg of hydrogen is negligible next to agriculture, but the export projects sit in arid regions chosen for their sun and wind, so they need seawater desalination, which adds capital cost, energy and a brine disposal problem.
slide_title: Challenges for Hydrogen as an Energy Carrier

prompt: Hydrogen has an energy density of 33.33 kWh_LHV/kg and, liquefied, a density of 0.07 kg/l. Verify the volumetric energy density of 2.4 kWh/l given on the slide, compare it with diesel at about 10 kWh/l, and say what follows for transport and storage.
solution: The volumetric energy density is the gravimetric energy density multiplied by the density: 33.33 kWh/kg x 0.07 kg/l = 2.33 kWh/l, which is the 2.4 kWh/l printed on the slide within rounding of the density. Diesel carries roughly 10 kWh/l, so even liquid hydrogen needs about four times the volume for the same energy, and gaseous hydrogen at ambient conditions with a density of 0.09 g/l is hopeless as a store. This is the central logistical fact about hydrogen: per kilogram it is the best fuel there is, about 2.8 times the heating value of diesel, but per litre it is the worst. Every element of the hydrogen infrastructure - compression to 700 bar, liquefaction at -253 °C, binding to a LOHC or conversion to ammonia - is a way of buying volumetric density with energy and with equipment.

prompt: The map shows hydrogen production potential for 2050 with cost categories and marks the demand centres. What does the factor of 5 refer to, which regions are the cheap producers, and which conclusion does the lecture draw?
solution: The colour scale gives the production cost, from below 1.00 $/kg (competitive for exports to any market) through 1.00-1.20, 1.20-1.80 and 1.80-2.50 up to above 2.50 $/kg, where production is uncompetitive against imports; between the cheapest and the most expensive location that is roughly a factor of 5. The large cheap potentials lie in the sun and wind belts: South America with 864 Mt/a, North Africa with 597 Mt/a, Australia with 380 Mt/a, the Middle East with 290 Mt/a and Namibia together with South Africa. The demand centres marked in blue are Europe, China, Japan and South Korea, India and the United States - and Japan and South Korea fall into the most expensive category, so they cannot produce competitively at all. The conclusion printed on the slide is that the best production locations and the demand centres do not coincide, so hydrogen transport is required; this is the bridge to the transport part of the chapter, where pipeline against ship and the chemical form of the molecule are discussed.

prompt: Name the four chemical reaction equations: Haber-Bosch, water-gas shift, electrolysis and steam reforming.
solution:
Steam reforming (SMR): CH4 + H2O → CO + 3 H2
Endothermic; the reaction heat comes from burning methane and part of the hydrogen with air, which also supplies the nitrogen for the ammonia synthesis. This is step 1 of conventional (grey) ammonia and the dominant route to hydrogen today.

Water-gas shift: CO + H2O → CO2 + H2
The carbon monoxide is reacted with further steam to raise the hydrogen yield. If the CO2 is captured here, the product is called blue hydrogen or blue ammonia.

Water electrolysis: 2 H2O → 2 H2 + O2
The renewable route. Alkaline about 4.7 kWh/Nm³ (≈ 64 % efficiency), SOEC about 3.6 kWh/Nm³ (≈ 83 %).

Haber-Bosch: N2 + 3 H2 → 2 NH3, ΔH° = −91.8 kJ/mol
At 400–450 °C and 120–220 bar over an iron catalyst; exothermic, but energy is needed for compression and pre-heating. Conversion per pass is below 20 %, limited by thermodynamics, so the ammonia is condensed out and the unreacted gas is recycled. Stoichiometrically 1 kg NH3 needs 0.18 kg H2 and 0.82 kg N2.

Sequence to remember: 1–2 make grey hydrogen from methane, 3 makes green hydrogen from water and power, 4 turns hydrogen into ammonia either way.

prompt: The consumption of an alkaline electrolyser, the efficiency of the liquefaction plant and the daily consumption of the ship are given. Determine the overall efficiency of transporting hydrogen over 10 days.
solution:
Work through the chain step by step and multiply the efficiencies; the exercise sheet does exactly this for a 20-day voyage.

1. Electrolysis. Alkaline needs 4.7 kWh/Nm³. With a density of 0.0899 kg/Nm³ that is 4.7 / 0.0899 = 52.28 kWh_el per kg H2. Against the lower heating value of 33.33 kWh/kg the efficiency is 33.33 / 52.28 = 63.8 %.

2. Liquefaction. 7 kWh_el per kg H2 on top. For 1 MWh of electricity available for electrolysis and liquefaction combined:
1,000 kWh / (52.28 + 7) kWh/kg = 16.87 kg H2, containing 16.87 · 33.33 = 562.2 kWh.
Efficiency up to the ship: 562.2 / 1,000 = 56.2 %.

3. Voyage. Liquid hydrogen boils off continuously at 0.2 % per day. After 10 days:
16.87 kg · 0.998^10 = 16.54 kg, i.e. 551.3 kWh.
(The sheet's 20-day case gives 16.87 · 0.998^20 = 16.21 kg / 540.2 kWh.)

Overall efficiency over 10 days = 551.3 / 1,000 = 55.1 %.

The comparison the exercise is really after: the same 1 MWh routed through electrolysis, air separation and Haber-Bosch yields 100.95 kg of ammonia with 521.9 kWh, and ammonia has no boil-off problem. Hydrogen starts ahead and loses its lead the longer the voyage lasts.
note: The lecturer's own solution sheet writes "1,000 MWh_el" in the ammonia step — it has to be 1,000 kWh_el, otherwise the result of 100.95 kg NH3 does not follow. Use kWh throughout.

prompt: Characterise ammonia: physical properties, natural occurrence, production volume, uses and footprint. How is it made, and where does the hydrogen for it come from today?
solution:
Ammonia NH3 is an inorganic, colourless gas with a pungent smell, caustic and corrosive. It boils at -33.34 °C, so it liquefies at ambient pressure with only moderate refrigeration, or at about 10 bar at room temperature; as a liquid its density is 0.68 kg/l. It occurs naturally, for example in the decomposition of dead plants and in animal excrement.

With a global production of 150 Mt/a it is one of the most common chemicals in the world. 85 % of it goes into fertiliser production, which is why ammonia is the molecule that feeds roughly half of humanity. Its production causes about 0.5 GtCO2/a, roughly 1 % of global carbon emissions, because the hydrogen comes from steam reforming of natural gas rather than from electrolysis.

It is produced by the Haber-Bosch process, N2 + 3 H2 -> 2 NH3.

One caveat on the slide: it states that 45 % of global hydrogen demand goes into ammonia. That does not square with the other figures of the lecture. 150 Mt/a of ammonia needs 150 * 0.18 = 27 Mt of hydrogen, which is about a quarter of the roughly 110 Mt/a of hydrogen produced globally, not 45 %. Quote the order of magnitude - ammonia is, after refining, the single largest hydrogen consumer - and derive the share stoichiometrically if you are asked for a number.

prompt: Characterise methanol: properties, natural occurrence, production volume and uses, the conventional production route and its footprint.
solution:
Methanol CH3OH is an organic, volatile, flammable liquid - an alcohol - colourless with a typical alcoholic odour. It boils at 65 °C and has a density of 0.79 kg/l, so it is a liquid at ambient pressure and temperature, which is the decisive practical advantage over both hydrogen and ammonia. It occurs naturally, for example as a metabolic product of bacteria and phytoplankton.

Global production is about 98 Mt/a. Methanol is mainly a chemical precursor, above all for formaldehyde and plastics, and about 30 % is used as fuel or as a blending component. Conventionally it is produced by hydrogenation of natural-gas-based carbon monoxide, CO + 2 H2 -> CH3OH, which is exothermic. Its production causes about 0.3 GtCO2/a.

One blemish in the slides: the enthalpy of the methanol synthesis is given as ΔH0 = -91.8 kJ/mol, exactly the value the slides also give for the Haber-Bosch reaction. The textbook value for CO + 2 H2 -> CH3OH is about -90.5 kJ/mol, so the figure looks copied from the ammonia slide. It does not change the argument - both reactions are exothermic and both are equilibrium-limited at the temperature the catalyst needs, which is why both run at high pressure with a recycle loop - but if you are asked for the number, quote it as roughly -90 kJ/mol.

prompt: Methanol is a liquid at ambient conditions, with a boiling point of 65 °C and a density of ___ kg/l.
solution: 0.79 kg/l. Together with the lower heating value of 5.83 kWh/kg this gives the volumetric energy density of about 4.7 kWh_LHV/l quoted on the following slide, roughly twice that of liquid hydrogen (2.4 kWh/l) and about 45 % above liquid ammonia (3.2 kWh/l). Being a liquid at ambient pressure and temperature is what allows the potential re-use of mineral oil infrastructure: ordinary tanks, ordinary tankers, ordinary pumps and ordinary bunkering equipment - no cryogenics, no pressure vessels, no toxic gas cloud.

prompt: Methanol as an energy carrier: give the energy density and hydrogen content, describe how the hydrogen is recovered, where the carbon comes from, and how methanol can be used directly.
solution:
Methanol carries 5.83 kWh_LHV/kg and 4.7 kWh_LHV/l and contains 12.5 wt.% hydrogen. Volumetrically it is the best of the carriers in this chapter - about twice liquid hydrogen and some 45 % above liquid ammonia - and it achieves that at ambient pressure and temperature.

Hydrogen is recovered by cracking, i.e. steam reforming of methanol, which the slide puts at high pressure of 50 - 100 bar and temperatures of 600 - 900 °C, with an energy demand of about 4.5 kWh_th/kgH2 and 3.2 kWh_el/kgH2. Thermally that is less than half of ammonia cracking; electrically it is about twice as much.

The carbon is the crux. Methanol is organic, so the CO2 must come from direct air capture, from a point source, or from biomass gasification. Only then is the fuel potentially carbon neutral - and the lecture is deliberately careful with the wording: potentially carbon neutral, not zero carbon, because the carbon is released again on combustion and a fossil point source merely delays the emission by one use.

Direct use is easy: in an internal combustion engine as an admixture to gasoline or as pure M100, or in a direct methanol fuel cell; and methanol derivatives such as biodiesel are already used as fuel in significant quantities.

One caveat on the slide: the cracking conditions of 50 - 100 bar and 600 - 900 °C are the ones given for ammonia. Industrial methanol steam reforming actually runs much milder, at roughly 250 - 350 °C, and that mildness is one of methanol's genuine advantages over ammonia. Quote the slide's numbers if asked, but know the physical point.

prompt: Write down the methanation reaction, state its thermodynamics and operating window, and give the stoichiometric input per kilogram of methane. Which efficiency does the lecture quote and at which TRL is the technology?
solution: Methanation runs the Sabatier process: 4 H2 + CO2 -> CH4 + 2 H2O. The reaction is highly exothermic with dH0 = -164.9 kJ/mol, so the reactor has to be cooled and the reaction heat is a by-product that should be used elsewhere. It operates at 300 - 450 °C and 1 - 5 bar. The efficiency is about 80 %, against a theoretical limit of 83 % - the gap to 100 % is exactly the reaction enthalpy that leaves the reactor as heat. Stoichiometrically 1 kg of CH4 needs 0.50 kg H2 and 2.74 kg CO2, which is why methanation always has to be paired with a carbon source; the complete power-to-methane chain is therefore CO2 capture + electrolysis + synthesis. The lecture places methanation at TRL 7, system prototype demonstration in an operational environment.

prompt: The catalytic production of methane from H2 and CO2 is called ___, whereas the anaerobic digestion of organic matter by microorganisms is called methanisation.
solution: Methanation, i.e. the Sabatier reaction. The lecture insists on this distinction: methanation is the catalytic Sabatier process 4 H2 + CO2 -> CH4 + 2 H2O at 300 - 450 °C, whereas methanisation is the biological route, the anaerobic digestion of organic matter by microorganisms that produces biogas.

prompt: Which statement about the Sabatier methanation reaction 4 H2 + CO2 -> CH4 + 2 H2O is correct?
options: It is endothermic (dH0 = +164.9 kJ/mol) and therefore needs a high-temperature heat supply.
It is highly exothermic (dH0 = -164.9 kJ/mol) and runs at 300 - 450 °C and 1 - 5 bar.
It runs at ambient temperature but requires 200 - 300 bar, like the Haber-Bosch synthesis.
It produces methane and oxygen, so no separate carbon source is needed.
solution: Methanation is highly exothermic, dH0 = -164.9 kJ/mol, and the lecture gives 300 - 450 °C and 1 - 5 bar as the operating window. The endothermic variant inverts the sign: the reaction releases heat, it does not consume it, and that released enthalpy is the main efficiency loss (about 80 % efficiency, theoretical limit 83 %). The high-pressure variant confuses methanation with Haber-Bosch, which does need 150 - 300 bar. The last option is wrong twice: the products are methane and water, not oxygen, and 2.74 kg of CO2 are needed per kilogram of methane, so a carbon source is indispensable.

prompt: What is a LOHC? Name the molecule pairs the lecture gives, the key figures, and the two process steps with their conditions.
solution:
A liquid organic hydrogen carrier is a liquid organic compound - a "carrier oil" - that can reversibly bond hydrogen. It is organic, but there is no CO2 release, because the carbon stays in the carrier molecule and the carrier is reused: it is a container, not a fuel. LOHCs are viscous liquids with flow characteristics similar to mineral oil, and many of them are by-products of oil refining.

The pairs, always given as lean form / rich form: methylcyclohexane MCH with toluol TOL; dibenzyltoluol H0-DBT with perhydro-dibenzyltoluol H18-DBT; benzyltoluol H0-BT (C14H14) with perhydro-benzyltoluol H12-BT (C14H26); and N-ethylcarbazole NEC with dodecahydro-N-ethylcarbazole DNEC. The number in the name counts the hydrogen atoms bound: H0-DBT is empty, H18-DBT is fully loaded with 18 hydrogen atoms, i.e. nine H2 molecules.

Key figures: energy density about 2 kWh/kg and 1.6 kWh/l, with a hydrogen content of 4 - 7 wt.% - the lowest of all the carriers, because the heavy carrier molecule has to be transported in both directions.

Process: exothermal hydrogenation at 30 - 50 bar and 150 - 200 °C in the exporting country, and endothermic dehydrogenation to release the hydrogen at about 250 - 400 °C, costing 9 - 14 kWh/kgH2, in the importing country. That asymmetry is the whole economics of LOHC: the heat is released where energy is cheap and required where energy is expensive.

prompt: The slide shows an 'innovative' Fischer-Tropsch chain with one box fewer than the conventional one. What has been merged, how does it work, and what is gained?
solution: The conventional PtL chain has four steps: CO2 capture - electrolysis - syngas production (rWGS) - FT synthesis. In the innovative chain the middle two are merged into a single box labelled 'Electrolysis & Syngas Production', so only three boxes remain: CO2 capture - electrolysis and syngas production - synthesis (FT process). The mechanism is high-temperature co-electrolysis in a solid oxide cell: water and captured CO2 are fed into the same stack and reduced simultaneously to H2 and CO, so renewable syngas leaves the electrolyser ready for the FT reactor. Because there is only one reactor and no separate endothermic rWGS stage that has to be heated and integrated, conversion losses are minimal and one whole process stage with its capital cost disappears. The commercial example is Sunfire's 'SynLink SOEC', whose flow picture reads: renewable electricity plus water plus captured CO2 into the SOEC, renewable syngas (CO + H2) out.

prompt: For hydrogen, ammonia and methanol: in which transport and storage options can existing infrastructure be re-used — ship, pipeline, underground storage?
solution:
From the comparison table of H2 derivatives:

Hydrogen. Ship: no re-use — there is only one prototype carrier of 2,200 dwt. Pipeline: re-use possible, repurposing existing natural gas pipelines costs 10–35 % of new construction. Underground storage: possible in salt caverns, which is the storage option the lecture discusses; porous formations are far less proven for hydrogen. Storage in tanks needs refrigeration or high pressure.

Ammonia. Ship: established, ships up to 75,000 dwt, and 126 ammonia terminals already exist; LPG carriers can be re-used. Pipeline: no re-use of gas pipelines. Storage: refrigerated or pressure tanks; established practice from the fertiliser industry.

Methanol. Ship: established, with potential re-use of oil tankers — the table gives no size limit in the methanol column; the "> 500,000 dwt" figure belongs to LOHCs and Fischer-Tropsch fuels. Pipeline: compatibility unclear. Storage: high compatibility — liquid at ambient conditions, so ordinary product tanks work.

The pattern behind the table: the more a molecule behaves like an existing fuel, the more infrastructure it inherits. Methanol and Fischer-Tropsch fuels inherit the oil world, SNG inherits the entire natural gas world, ammonia inherits the LPG and fertiliser world — and pure hydrogen inherits almost nothing and has to be built from scratch.

prompt: Reproduce the energy-density scatter plot: what is on each axis, roughly where do LOHC, ammonia, methanol, liquefied methane, syn-fuels and hydrogen sit, and what is the trade-off the plot is meant to show?
solution: The x-axis is the gravimetric energy density in kWhLHV/kg from 0 to 35, the y-axis the volumetric energy density in kWhLHV/l from 0 to 10, and every carrier is one dot. Hydrogen sits at the far right: liquid hydrogen at about 33 kWh/kg but only 2.4 kWh/l, and hydrogen compressed to 700 bar at the same gravimetric value with an even lower 1.3 kWh/l. LOHC is in the bottom left corner at about 2.1 kWh/kg and 1.6 kWh/l. Ammonia is at about 5.2 kWh/kg and 3.2 kWh/l, methanol at about 5.8 kWh/kg and 4.7 kWh/l; wood and lignite sit near them at about 5 kWh/kg and 2 - 4.3 kWh/l, hard coal at about 8 kWh/kg and 6.6 kWh/l. Liquefied methane is at 13.9 kWh/kg and 6.3 kWh/l. The best volumetric performers are the liquid hydrocarbons: syn-kerosene and syn-diesel at about 11.5 - 12 kWh/kg and 9.6 - 9.7 kWh/l, syn-gasoline slightly lower at 8.5 kWh/l. The trade-off: hydrogen wins by mass by a factor of about three but loses by volume by a factor of four, and because ships, aircraft and tanks are volume-limited rather than mass-limited, the derivatives that bind hydrogen into a carbon chain occupy the useful upper-middle corner. No carrier reaches both a high gravimetric and a high volumetric density - that is precisely why derivatives exist.

prompt: In the energy-density diagram, which carrier occupies the point of highest gravimetric but lowest volumetric energy density?
options: Liquid hydrogen
LOHC
Liquefied methane
Syn-kerosene
solution: Liquid hydrogen: about 33 kWh/kg, the highest gravimetric density of any chemical fuel, but only 2.4 kWh/l; hydrogen at 700 bar is even worse volumetrically at roughly 1.3 kWh/l. LOHC is the opposite kind of extreme - poor on both axes at about 2.1 kWh/kg and 1.6 kWh/l, because the carrier molecule itself is dead weight that has to be shipped in both directions. Liquefied methane is the mid-field compromise at 13.9 kWh/kg and 6.3 kWh/l, and syn-kerosene is the volumetric winner at about 9.6 kWh/l with 11.5 kWh/kg.

prompt: The chart on the shipping-fleet slide gives the share of fuels in the world fleet by gross tonnage for June 2022, July 2023 and June 2024. Which reading is correct?
options: Alternative fuels are dominated by battery/hybrid propulsion, which reached 6.65 % in 2024.
The alternative-fuel share is stagnating at about 5.5 % because LNG is being phased out.
Conventional fuels fall from 94.5 % to 92.6 %, alternative fuels rise from 5.5 % to 7.4 %, and almost all of the alternative share is LNG (6.65 % in 2024).
Conventional fuels have already fallen below 80 %, with methanol as the largest alternative at 6.65 %.
solution: The bars read 94.5 %, 93.5 % and 92.6 % for conventional fuels and 5.5 %, 6.52 % and 7.4 % for alternative fuels in total. Within the alternative share LNG alone accounts for 5.39 %, 5.96 % and 6.65 %, i.e. roughly 90 % of everything that is not conventional. The rest is marginal: battery/hybrid 0.06 %, 0.26 % and 0.32 %, LPG 0.06 %, 0.25 % and 0.37 %, and methanol only 0.02 %, 0.05 % and 0.09 %. Three lessons follow: the transition has barely started in the existing fleet, the only alternative fuel with real market share is LNG - a fossil fuel that improves CO2 only marginally and adds a methane-slip risk - and methanol, despite dominating the orderbook, is still statistically invisible in the fleet, because an orderbook takes a decade to become a fleet.

prompt: The metals slide re-draws the energy-density diagram with iron and aluminium added. Where do the metals sit relative to the chemical fuels, and what does that position imply for their use?
solution: The axes are the same as before - gravimetric energy density in kWhLHV/kg on the x-axis, volumetric in kWhLHV/l on the y-axis - but the y-axis now runs to 25 instead of 10, because the metals break the old scale. Aluminium sits at about 8.6 kWh/kg and 23.5 kWh/l, by far the highest volumetric density on the chart, with aluminium powder lower at about 14 kWh/l because a powder bed contains voids. Iron sits at about 2.05 kWh/kg and 16.1 kWh/l, with iron powder at roughly 9.7 kWh/l for the same reason. Compare that with the best chemical fuels: syn-kerosene at about 9.6 kWh/l, liquefied methane at 6.3 kWh/l and liquid hydrogen at only 2.4 kWh/l. Gravimetrically the metals are poor - iron at 2.05 kWh/kg is at the level of an LOHC and about one sixteenth of hydrogen - but volumetrically they beat every fuel on the chart. The implication is exactly the application profile the lecture names: metals are attractive where volume and storability matter and mass does not, i.e. seasonal storage in a heap, bulk shipping in existing carriers, and firing a retrofitted coal power plant; they are unattractive wherever the fuel has to be carried along, which rules out aviation and most road transport. Note that the powder values are the ones that count in practice, since a burner is fed with powder and not with a solid block.
